modules.title: Respiratory histology · Lab 2
modules.summary: Identify airways, gas-exchange units, alveolar cells and pleura from the supplied microscopy.

topics.title: Orient a tracheal section
body: Begin at low power: a large airway with a C-shaped hyaline cartilage ring lies anterior to the esophagus. The open posterior ends are bridged by trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic tissue, allowing the esophagus to expand.

Work from lumen outward: respiratory epithelium plus lamina propria form the mucosa; the submucosa contains vessels and seromucous glands; hyaline cartilage supports patency; an outer adventitial connective tissue layer anchors the airway. The supplied text lists three layers although it describes a four-layer wall; do not omit the outer adventitia.
keyPoints: C-shaped cartilage: trachea
Posterior gap: trachealis
Seromucous glands: submucosa

questions.question: A tracheal section has a posterior gap in its C-shaped cartilage. What bridges this gap?
options: Trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic tissue
reasons: The diaphragm is the main inspiratory muscle below the thorax, not the posterior tracheal wall.
Trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic tissue bridge the posterior cartilage ends beside the esophagus.
Visceral pleura covers the lung surface, not the tracheal gap.
The characteristic tracheal ring is incomplete posteriorly, so cartilage does not bridge the gap.
questions.explanation: Trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic tissue bridge the posterior cartilage ends beside the esophagus.

questions.question: Which location contains the tracheal seromucous acini described in this lab?
reasons: Alveolar septa contain capillaries and thin gas-exchange tissue, not tracheal glands.
Cartilage matrix contains chondrocytes and provides support; glands lie outside it.
The pleural cavity is a potential fluid-lubricated space around the lung.
The tracheal submucosa contains connective tissue, vessels and seromucous glands.
questions.explanation: The tracheal submucosa contains connective tissue, vessels and seromucous glands.

topics.title: Recognize an intrapulmonary bronchus
body: A bronchus inside lung parenchyma has discontinuous cartilage plates rather than the tracheal C-shaped ring. Its folded mucosa reflects the circumferential smooth muscle layer; large bronchi also have submucosal glands.

Trace the wall outward: pseudostratified respiratory epithelium, loose lamina propria, smooth muscle, gland-bearing submucosa, irregular hyaline cartilage plates and adventitia continuous with the lung. Use several features together; a section can miss one cartilage plate.
keyPoints: Cartilage plates and glands support bronchus identification
Muscle produces mucosal folds
Do not diagnose bronchiole from one cartilage-free field

questions.question: Which additional wall finding would most strongly confirm a bronchus rather than a bronchiole when examining this airway?
options: Pleural mesothelium at the organ surface
Hyaline cartilage plates in an airway wall
A common chamber surrounded by alveoli
reasons: Thin squamous lining is characteristic of alveoli rather than a large conducting airway.
Mesothelium marks a pleural surface, not the wall of this airway.
Cartilage plates surrounding an airway in lung tissue distinguish a bronchus from a bronchiole.
A shared opening of alveoli describes an alveolar sac, which lacks a cartilaginous airway wall.
questions.explanation: Cartilage plates surrounding an airway in lung tissue distinguish a bronchus from a bronchiole.

figure.caption: Intrapulmonary airway micrograph; supplied histology lab p7, left field

questions.question: Why can a bronchial mucosa look folded in cross-section?
options: Contraction of the circumferential smooth muscle
Replacement of cartilage by alveolar sacs
Contraction of skeletal muscle in the mucosa
reasons: Bronchial smooth muscle changes airway caliber and produces mucosal folds.
Alveolar sacs belong to the distal respiratory zone and do not create bronchial folds.
The relevant muscle layer is smooth, not skeletal.
Pneumothorax separates pleural surfaces; it is not the normal cause of bronchial mucosal folds.
questions.explanation: Bronchial smooth muscle changes airway caliber and produces mucosal folds.

figure.caption: Practical reference image · Histology of respiratory tract 2_Dr. Einas.key, p/slide 6

topics.title: Separate bronchioles from bronchi
body: Bronchioles have no cartilage plates or submucosal glands. Their wall includes smooth muscle, a loose elastic lamina propria and adventitial connective tissue attached to surrounding lung. The lining becomes lower, from ciliated columnar toward cuboidal in smaller airways, with increasing club cells.

At low power find the lumen, muscle and surrounding alveoli. Then scan the entire wall and adjacent tissue before calling cartilage absent. Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting branches; alveoli opening from an airway identify a respiratory bronchiole instead.
keyPoints: Bronchiole: no cartilage, no glands
Club cells increase distally
Terminal bronchiole conducts; respiratory bronchiole also exchanges gas

questions.question: In this small-airway field, which combination favors a bronchiole?
options: Cartilage plates and abundant submucosal glands
Smooth muscle with no cartilage plates or glands
A C-shaped cartilage ring and posterior trachealis
Only mesothelium and an underlying collagen layer
reasons: Cartilage and glands favor an intrapulmonary bronchus.
A smooth muscle wall lacking cartilage and glands fits a bronchiole; confirm by surveying the whole section.
A C-shaped ring and posterior trachealis identify trachea.
Mesothelium over connective tissue identifies pleura rather than an airway.
questions.explanation: A smooth muscle wall lacking cartilage and glands fits a bronchiole; confirm by surveying the whole section.

figure.caption: Small airway micrograph; supplied histology lab p7, right field

questions.question: Which cell population becomes more prominent as bronchioles become smaller?
reasons: Chondrocytes live in cartilage, which is absent from bronchioles.
Bronchiolar walls lack submucosal glands.
Mesothelial cells line the pleura rather than distal conducting airways.
Club cells increase distally as the bronchiolar epithelium becomes lower.
questions.explanation: Club cells increase distally as the bronchiolar epithelium becomes lower.

activities.prompt: Match the airway to its strongest wall feature

pairs.definition: C-shaped hyaline cartilage with posterior trachealis
Discontinuous cartilage plates; glands in larger branches
Smooth muscle without cartilage plates or glands

figure.caption: Practical reference image · Histology of respiratory tract 2_Dr. Einas.key, p/slide 10

topics.title: Trace respiratory bronchiole → duct → sac
body: A respiratory bronchiole retains segments of cuboidal epithelium with club cells and some cilia, interrupted by alveolar openings. Smooth muscle and elastic fibers remain.

An alveolar duct is an elongated passage whose peripheral boundary is almost entirely alveolar openings; small smooth muscle rings lie in the knobs of intervening septa. An alveolar sac is a shared space surrounded by a cluster of alveoli, often at a duct termination. An alveolus is one thin-walled gas-exchange chamber.
keyPoints: Alveoli interrupt a respiratory bronchiole wall
Duct: elongated passage bordered by alveoli
Sac: common space shared by a cluster

questions.question: What finding distinguishes a respiratory bronchiole from a terminal bronchiole?
options: An alveolar opening interrupts the epithelial wall
A hyaline cartilage ring surrounds the lumen
A submucosal seromucous gland is present
reasons: Alveoli opening directly from the bronchiolar wall indicate the start of the respiratory zone.
Neither terminal nor respiratory bronchioles normally has cartilage.
Submucosal glands support bronchus rather than bronchiole identification.
Mesothelium belongs to pleura; it does not replace bronchiolar lining.
questions.explanation: Alveoli opening directly from the bronchiolar wall indicate the start of the respiratory zone.

figure.caption: Respiratory bronchiole and alveolar openings · lab p8

questions.question: An elongated passage is bordered almost entirely by alveoli, with smooth muscle knobs at septal tips. Identify it.
reasons: A terminal bronchiole has a continuous conducting epithelial wall without alveolar openings.
A pulmonary vein is lined by endothelium and carries blood; alveoli do not open into it.
These are the characteristic wall and shape of an alveolar duct.
Trachea has respiratory mucosa, glands and cartilage, not a boundary made of alveoli.
questions.explanation: These are the characteristic wall and shape of an alveolar duct.

questions.question: How does an alveolar sac differ from one alveolus?
options: It has a C-shaped cartilage wall
It is a common space surrounded by several alveoli
It is lined by pseudostratified epithelium
It is the connective tissue outside visceral pleura
reasons: Cartilage is absent from both alveolar sacs and alveoli.
A sac is a shared chamber into which a cluster of individual alveoli opens.
Thin alveolar epithelium, not pseudostratified respiratory lining, forms these distal units.
The sac is an air space in lung parenchyma, not tissue external to pleura.
questions.explanation: A sac is a shared chamber into which a cluster of individual alveoli opens.

figure.caption: Practical reference image · Histology of respiratory tract 2_Dr. Einas.key, p/slide 15

topics.title: Identify alveolar cells and capillaries
body: Alveoli bring air beside a dense capillary network. Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous cells forming the principal epithelial gas-exchange surface. Their flattened shape minimizes diffusion distance.

Type II pneumocytes are more cuboidal, often at septal junctions and bulging into the airspace. They secrete surfactant and serve as progenitors for alveolar epithelial repair. A capillary lumen with erythrocytes belongs to the blood side, not to an alveolar airspace.
keyPoints: Type I: thin diffusion surface
Type II: cuboidal, surfactant, epithelial repair
Capillary: erythrocytes in a vascular lumen

questions.question: In the numbered source micrograph, cell 2 is cuboidal and bulges at a septal junction. Which function matches it?
options: Forms cartilage to hold the alveolus open
Secretes surfactant and supports alveolar epithelial repair
reasons: Alveolar walls do not contain supporting cartilage.
Alveolar pneumocytes do not form a mucociliary escalator.
Pleural mesothelium, not alveolar type II cells, lines the lubricated pleural surface.
A cuboidal type II pneumocyte produces surfactant and can replace alveolar epithelial cells.
questions.explanation: A cuboidal type II pneumocyte produces surfactant and can replace alveolar epithelial cells.

figure.caption: Numbered alveolar cells and capillaries · lab p11

questions.question: Which alveolar cell is best adapted for minimizing the diffusion distance for oxygen?
reasons: The very thin squamous type I pneumocyte forms the main epithelial diffusion surface.
Goblet cells secrete mucus in conducting airways; they are not the thin alveolar barrier.
Club cells are nonciliated secretory bronchiolar cells.
Type II cells supply surfactant and repair; their cuboidal shape is less suited to a minimal diffusion barrier.
questions.explanation: The very thin squamous type I pneumocyte forms the main epithelial diffusion surface.

activities.prompt: The cuboidal alveolar cell that makes surfactant is the type ___ pneumocyte.
activities.explanation: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant; type I cells provide the very thin gas-exchange lining.

figure.caption: Practical reference image · Histology of respiratory tract 2_Dr. Einas.key, p/slide 19

topics.title: Recognize the visceral pleural surface
body: At the edge of the lung, identify a thin layer of simple squamous mesothelial cells over connective tissue containing collagen and elastic fibers. Unlike an internal alveolar wall, this is the organ surface.

The mesothelium contributes a lubricating serous film so pleural surfaces slide during breathing. Its connective tissue attaches it to lung parenchyma and permits flexibility. Distinguish an external mesothelial surface from capillary endothelium inside a septum.
keyPoints: Visceral pleura: mesothelium + fibroelastic connective tissue
Position at lung surface is essential
Serous film reduces friction

questions.question: The arrows at the external lung surface point to a thin simple squamous layer. What is it?
reasons: Respiratory epithelium lines conducting airways and is taller and often ciliated.
Type II cells are cuboidal alveolar epithelial cells rather than the external pleural lining.
Simple squamous mesothelium covers the visceral pleura over fibroelastic connective tissue.
Cartilage has chondrocytes in matrix and is not a one-cell surface lining.
questions.explanation: Simple squamous mesothelium covers the visceral pleura over fibroelastic connective tissue.

figure.caption: Visceral pleura mesothelium and connective tissue · lab p12

questions.question: What is the primary mechanical benefit of the pleural serous film?
reasons: The film permits sliding rather than preventing movement.
The lubricating film allows pleural surfaces to move with minimal friction.
Alveolar surfactant reduces air–liquid surface tension inside alveoli, a different location and role.
Serous fluid does not contract; respiratory muscles generate movement.
questions.explanation: The lubricating film allows pleural surfaces to move with minimal friction.

figure.caption: Practical reference image · Histology of respiratory tract 2_Dr. Einas.key, p/slide 28

modules.title: Intercostal space · Anatomy lab
modules.summary: Identify muscle planes, neurovascular bundles, arterial anastomoses, venous drainage and atypical nerves.

topics.title: Find the neurovascular plane
body: Identify external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles from superficial to deep. The principal intercostal nerve and vessels travel between internal and innermost layers, close to the inferior border of the rib above.

The principal bundle is ordered vein–artery–nerve from superior to inferior in the costal groove. A smaller collateral branch runs lower in the space. External intercostals elevate ribs; interosseous internal intercostals help depress ribs in forced expiration, while parasternal portions can assist inspiration. Subcostales span more than one space posteriorly; transversus thoracis lies behind the sternum.
keyPoints: Superficial → deep: external, internal, innermost
Principal bundle: internal–innermost plane
VAN from above downward; collateral branch lower

questions.question: Between which two muscle layers does the principal intercostal neurovascular bundle travel?
reasons: The principal bundle lies deeper than the external–internal interval.
The bundle lies superficial to innermost intercostal, not deep to it or beside visceral pleura.
That superficial interval does not contain the principal intercostal bundle.
The main nerve and vessels travel in the plane between internal and innermost intercostals.
questions.explanation: The main nerve and vessels travel in the plane between internal and innermost intercostals.

questions.question: From superior to inferior in the main costal groove, the order is:
reasons: VAN is the order under the rib: vein superior, artery middle, nerve inferior.
This reverses the superior–inferior order.
The artery lies below the vein, not above it.
The nerve lies below the artery, not between artery and vein.
questions.explanation: VAN is the order under the rib: vein superior, artery middle, nerve inferior.

questions.question: Locate the bundle in the illustrated muscle layers. Which pair of muscles bounds its main plane?
reasons: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between these layers.
The illustrated bundle lies deeper than this interval.
The main bundle runs superficial to the innermost layer.
questions.explanation: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between these layers.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering

activities.prompt: The main bundle lies between the internal and ___ intercostal muscles.
activities.explanation: The neurovascular plane is between internal and innermost intercostal layers; a collateral bundle may also be present.

figure.caption: Practical reference image · CVP-Lab- Intercostal space. Dr Atif Mazhar.pdf.pdf, p/slide 4

topics.title: Trace posterior arterial supply
body: There are eleven pairs of posterior intercostal arteries. The first two spaces are supplied through the superior (supreme) intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. Spaces 3–11 receive branches of the descending thoracic aorta.

Trace a posterior artery around the space and find its dorsal, muscular, cutaneous and collateral branches. The collateral branch runs at a lower level and joins an anterior vessel. The right aortic branches have a longer course across the vertebral bodies because the descending aorta lies on the left.
keyPoints: Spaces 1–2: superior intercostal → costocervical trunk
Spaces 3–11: descending thoracic aorta
Collateral branch runs lower in the space

questions.question: The second posterior intercostal artery most directly belongs to which supply route?
reasons: The superior epigastric is a terminal internal thoracic branch, not the route to the second posterior space.
The upper two posterior spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal branch of the costocervical trunk.
The musculophrenic supplies anterior spaces 7–9 and arises from internal thoracic, not descending aorta.
The lateral thoracic artery is not the listed posterior intercostal source.
questions.explanation: The upper two posterior spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal branch of the costocervical trunk.

questions.question: A posterior intercostal artery in the eighth space usually arises from the:
reasons: Superior epigastric supplies the anterior abdominal wall.
The superior intercostal supplies the upper two posterior spaces.
Posterior spaces 3–11 arise from the descending thoracic aorta.
Pulmonary arteries supply lung gas-exchange capillaries, not the thoracic wall.
questions.explanation: Posterior spaces 3–11 arise from the descending thoracic aorta.

questions.question: Follow a vessel from the vertebral side into an intercostal space. Which connection joins it to the anterior supply?
options: Anastomosis with an anterior intercostal branch
Termination in the adjacent spinal nerve
reasons: This joins the posterior and anterior arterial routes within the space.
A venous confluence does not create the arterial collateral route shown.
The nerve follows the vascular plane but does not carry arterial flow.
questions.explanation: This joins the posterior and anterior arterial routes within the space.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering
Anterior/posterior arterial anastomoses and collateral branches · lab p8

topics.title: Connect anterior vessels and internal thoracic branches
body: Two anterior intercostal arteries run in each of spaces 1–9. In spaces 1–6 they arise from the internal thoracic artery; in spaces 7–9 they come from its musculophrenic branch. Spaces 10 and 11 have no anterior intercostal arteries.

The upper anterior artery joins the main posterior artery; the lower joins its collateral branch. The internal thoracic terminates as superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries. Superior epigastric enters the rectus sheath and anastomoses with inferior epigastric; musculophrenic follows the costal margin and supplies lower anterior spaces and diaphragm.
keyPoints: Anterior 1–6: internal thoracic
Anterior 7–9: musculophrenic
Anterior 10–11: absent
Upper joins main posterior; lower joins collateral

questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior intercostal arteries in the eighth space?
reasons: Musculophrenic supplies anterior intercostal arteries in spaces 7–9.
Descending aorta supplies posterior, not these anterior, branches.
Superior intercostal supplies posterior spaces 1–2.
Inferior epigastric is an abdominal wall vessel; it anastomoses with superior epigastric.
questions.explanation: Musculophrenic supplies anterior intercostal arteries in spaces 7–9.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the anterior vessels?
options: One artery supplies each of all eleven spaces
Spaces 10 and 11 are supplied by anterior branches of the aorta
The lower anterior artery joins only a pulmonary artery
Two anterior arteries occur in spaces 1–9
reasons: The handout describes two anterior arteries in the upper nine spaces.
The last two spaces have no anterior intercostal arteries.
The lower anterior artery joins the collateral posterior branch, not a pulmonary artery.
There are two anterior arteries per space in spaces 1–9; spaces 10–11 lack them.
questions.explanation: There are two anterior arteries per space in spaces 1–9; spaces 10–11 lack them.

activities.prompt: Match the artery to its territory

topics.title: Follow intercostal venous return
body: Anterior veins follow anterior arteries: the upper six spaces drain to internal thoracic veins and spaces 7–9 to musculophrenic veins. Posterior drainage is asymmetric. Lower posterior spaces drain through the azygos system: azygos on the right, hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos on the left.

The first posterior intercostal vein can drain to vertebral or brachiocephalic veins. The second and third, sometimes fourth, form a superior intercostal vein. The right superior intercostal joins azygos; the left crosses the aortic arch and drains to left brachiocephalic. Distinguish the superior intercostal vein from the superior intercostal artery.
keyPoints: Right posterior: azygos system
Left posterior: hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos
Left superior intercostal → left brachiocephalic

questions.question: The left superior intercostal vein normally drains to the:
reasons: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated lung blood to the left atrium, not this chest-wall venous trunk.
The left superior intercostal vein passes over the arch toward the left brachiocephalic vein.
Coronary sinus drains most cardiac venous blood.
Inferior epigastric veins drain abdominal wall territory, not the superior intercostal trunk.
questions.explanation: The left superior intercostal vein passes over the arch toward the left brachiocephalic vein.

questions.question: Which pairing matches lower posterior intercostal venous drainage?
options: Right → left brachiocephalic; left → coronary sinus
reasons: Intercostal wall veins belong to systemic venous return, not pulmonary veins.
These destinations do not describe the lower posterior chest wall.
The lower posterior spaces drain through the asymmetric azygos system.
Superior epigastric veins are anterior abdominal wall drainage, not the lower posterior route.
questions.explanation: The lower posterior spaces drain through the asymmetric azygos system.

questions.question: In the drainage diagram, follow the right posterior intercostal veins toward the central trunk. Which system receives them?
reasons: The right posterior drainage joins the azygos system on its way to the SVC.
This channel carries lymph toward the left venous angle.
This collects venous drainage from myocardium.
questions.explanation: The right posterior drainage joins the azygos system on its way to the SVC.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering
Intercostal venous drainage · lab p13

topics.title: Identify typical and atypical intercostal nerves
body: An intercostal nerve is an anterior ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve. Follow communicating branches to the sympathetic trunk, a collateral branch, lateral cutaneous branches and anterior cutaneous termination. A posterior ramus instead supplies deep back muscles and overlying skin.

T1 contributes mainly to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus; its small intercostal component lacks the usual cutaneous branches. T2 gives the intercostobrachial nerve to axillary floor and upper medial arm. T7–T11 continue into the abdominal wall as thoracoabdominal nerves. T12 runs below rib12 and is the subcostal nerve, rather than occupying an intercostal space.
keyPoints: Intercostal nerves are anterior rami
T1: brachial plexus contribution
T2: intercostobrachial
T7–T11: thoracoabdominal; T12: subcostal

questions.question: After axillary surgery a patient loses sensation over the axillary floor and upper medial arm. Which nerve in the lab is implicated?
reasons: The lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve supplying this area.
Phrenic supplies the diaphragm and central diaphragmatic/mediastinal sensory territory.
A posterior ramus supplies the back, not this axillary and medial-arm region.
T12 supplies the lower thoracoabdominal wall, not upper medial arm.
questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve supplying this area.

questions.question: Which anterior rami continue into the abdominal wall as thoracoabdominal nerves?
reasons: C3–C5 contribute to phrenic, not thoracoabdominal, innervation.
Most of T1 contributes to the brachial plexus.
S2–S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves are unrelated to these thoracic rami.
T7–T11 leave their intercostal spaces and continue to abdominal wall muscles and skin.
questions.explanation: T7–T11 leave their intercostal spaces and continue to abdominal wall muscles and skin.

questions.question: Trace the branch that leaves the intercostal nerve laterally and heads toward the skin. What is its role?
options: Cutaneous supply to the lateral thoracic wall
Preganglionic input to the sympathetic trunk
reasons: The lateral cutaneous branch leaves the main nerve and supplies overlying skin.
That course is through a communicating ramus near the vertebral column.
That action is supplied by the phrenic nerve.
questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous branch leaves the main nerve and supplies overlying skin.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering
Thoracic spinal nerve branches · lab p17

modules.title: Pulmonary function testing · Prelab
modules.summary: Prepare the spirometer, read tidal and forced recordings, calculate indices and interpret the supplied asthma case.

topics.title: Set up and zero before recording
body: The flow head measures airflow; the software also displays volume. Before recording, leave the flow head undisturbed on the bench and select Spirometer Pod from the flow-channel function menu, then Zero. Movement or airflow during zeroing can bias the baseline.

For quiet breathing, the handout asks the volunteer to face away from the screen so they do not consciously alter the pattern. Record normal tidal breathing for 20 seconds and annotate the trace. Equipment-specific steps here follow the supplied prelab, rather than being a universal device protocol.
keyPoints: Zero with flow head still on bench
Facing away reduces conscious control
Record and label quiet tidal breathing

questions.question: During zeroing a volunteer continues blowing through the flow head. What is the best correction?
options: Keep blowing harder to calibrate a maximal flow
Skip zeroing and use any baseline
Place the flow head undisturbed on the bench and re-zero
reasons: The zero step establishes no-flow baseline, not maximal flow.
An incorrect baseline can distort recorded flow and derived volume.
The supplied protocol specifies an undisturbed flow head on the bench during zeroing.
A setup artifact is not evidence of a ventilatory diagnosis.
questions.explanation: The supplied protocol specifies an undisturbed flow head on the bench during zeroing.

questions.question: Why does the prelab ask a volunteer to face away from the screen during quiet breathing?
options: To prevent light from changing the gas composition
To reduce conscious control of their breathing pattern
To make residual volume directly measurable
To eliminate the need for a mouthpiece
reasons: Screen light does not meaningfully change respiratory gas composition.
Watching a trace can change how a volunteer breathes, so facing away helps obtain spontaneous tidal breathing.
Orientation cannot make spirometry measure trapped residual volume.
A mouthpiece/flow head is still required for the measurement.
questions.explanation: Watching a trace can change how a volunteer breathes, so facing away helps obtain spontaneous tidal breathing.

topics.title: Read flow and volume; identify capacities
body: Read the axes first. A flow trace reports rate (L/s); the volume trace reports an accumulated change in liters. Tidal volume is the peak-to-trough volume excursion during a quiet breath, not the height of a flow peak.

After quiet breathing, a maximal inspiration above a normal inspiratory level demonstrates inspiratory reserve volume; maximal expiration below the resting expiratory level demonstrates expiratory reserve volume. IC=VT+IRV; VC=IRV+VT+ERV. Ordinary spirometry measures volume changes and cannot directly measure residual volume, FRC or TLC because each includes gas not exhaled into the spirometer.
keyPoints: Use volume axis for VT
IC=VT+IRV; VC=IRV+VT+ERV
RV-containing capacities require another method

questions.question: Quiet volume readings alternate between0.15 and0.65 L. What is the tidal volume?
reasons: Tidal volume is the excursion:0.65−0.15=0.50 L.
Adding the endpoints gives0.80 L but does not measure the breath excursion.
0.65 is an endpoint, and L/s is a flow unit rather than volume.
0.15 is the lower baseline value, not the difference between trough and peak.
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is the excursion:0.65−0.15=0.50 L.

questions.question: Which capacity cannot be measured directly with ordinary spirometry?
reasons: VC is a sum of volume changes that can be inhaled/exhaled through the device.
IC is the volume inspired from a resting expiration and can be recorded.
ERV is the extra volume expired below a resting expiration.
FRC=ERV+RV includes residual volume that remains in the lungs after maximal expiration.
questions.explanation: FRC=ERV+RV includes residual volume that remains in the lungs after maximal expiration.

questions.question: On the resting breathing trace, which measurement gives tidal volume for one breath?
options: The volume difference between an ordinary trough and its next peak
The horizontal distance from one peak to the next
The volume difference from the baseline to maximal forced expiration
reasons: The vertical excursion represents the volume moved during a quiet inspiration.
This is breath duration when the horizontal axis represents time.
That interval involves more than one quiet tidal excursion.
questions.explanation: The vertical excursion represents the volume moved during a quiet inspiration.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering

activities.prompt: VT=0.5 L and IRV=2.5 L. Enter IC in liters.
activities.explanation: IC=VT+IRV=0.5+2.5=3.0 L. It is a capacity, not a flow.

figure.caption: Extracted PFT prelab figure · slide 11

topics.title: Perform and read forced expiration
body: The prelab asks for re-zeroing,30 seconds of normal breathing, maximal inspiration, then expiration as forcefully and fully as possible until no more air can be expelled. Record three separate forced breaths. The initial maximal inspiration and sustained expiration matter: a weak start or early stop can produce misleading numbers.

FEV1 is the volume exhaled in the first second of the forced maneuver. FVC is the full forced vital capacity. On the supplied remaining-volume trace, both are downward differences from maximal inspiration, not absolute y-axis readings. FEV1/FVC=(first-second volume)/(total forced volume), expressed as a fraction or percent.
keyPoints: Start from maximal inspiration
FEV1: first second; FVC: full maneuver
Repeat to obtain three recordings

questions.question: A forced expiration expels2.4 L in the first second and4.0 L in total. What is FEV1/FVC?
reasons: 4.0/2.4 reverses the required ratio; neither1.67 nor1.67% is the correct result.
40% is the remaining fraction, not the exhaled first-second fraction.
Divide the first-second volume by the total forced volume:2.4/4.0=0.60=60%.
FEV1 is a volume; this question asks a dimensionless ratio, not flow.
questions.explanation: Divide the first-second volume by the total forced volume:2.4/4.0=0.60=60%.

questions.question: A subject starts the forced maneuver from a normal tidal inspiration instead of maximal inspiration. Why is this a problem?
options: The starting lung volume is inadequate for the intended vital-capacity maneuver
reasons: An incomplete inspiration can reduce measured volumes rather than guarantee normality.
The protocol requires maximal inspiration so the full forced vital capacity can be assessed.
Plethysmography is a different measurement technique; a changed breathing maneuver does not create it.
Residual volume remains in the lungs and is not directly recorded by ordinary spirometry.
questions.explanation: The protocol requires maximal inspiration so the full forced vital capacity can be assessed.

questions.question: On the forced-expiration recording, where do you read the first-second expired volume?
options: At one second after the start of the forced effort
At the final volume plateau regardless of elapsed time
At the highest instantaneous flow without considering elapsed time
reasons: FEV₁ is the volume expired by that time point.
The plateau corresponds to the full forced vital capacity.
Peak flow is a rate and differs from first-second volume.
questions.explanation: FEV₁ is the volume expired by that time point.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering
Extracted PFT prelab figure · slide 6

topics.title: Distinguish obstruction from suspected restriction
body: Obstruction makes rapid expiration difficult; FEV1 often falls disproportionately, lowering FEV1/FVC. A reduced FVC with a preserved ratio can suggest restriction but can also reflect poor effort or air trapping. Confirming restriction requires reduced TLC, measured with an appropriate lung-volume method.

Use the measured ratio against an appropriate lower limit of normal and inspect recording quality. A single low value or a simplistic fixed cutoff is not a complete diagnosis. Dyspnea can also have cardiac, hematologic or deconditioning causes, so normal spirometry does not rule out all causes of breathlessness.
keyPoints: Low FEV1/FVC supports airflow obstruction
Low FVC alone does not prove restriction
Inspect effort and repeatability first

questions.question: A technically adequate test has FEV1/FVC below the provided lower limit of normal. Which pattern is supported?
options: Confirmed restriction without any lung-volume measurement
reasons: A ratio below the appropriate lower limit supports expiratory airflow obstruction.
Restriction requires reduced TLC; the ratio alone does not confirm it.
A low ratio is an abnormal finding even if some individual values are near predicted.
Spirometry does not measure hemoglobin concentration or establish anemia.
questions.explanation: A ratio below the appropriate lower limit supports expiratory airflow obstruction.

questions.question: FVC is low but FEV1/FVC is preserved. What additional measurement is needed to confirm restriction?
reasons: Pulse rate does not determine the total amount of gas in the lungs.
Inspired oxygen fraction does not distinguish restriction from air trapping.
One flow measurement cannot confirm a reduction in total lung volume.
Restriction is confirmed by TLC below the relevant lower limit of normal.

topics.title: Apply the supplied asthma case
body: The case describes recurrent trigger-associated wheeze, increased attacks after infection and severe respiratory distress despite albuterol. Bronchial smooth muscle contraction, airway inflammation and mucus can obstruct expiratory airflow and promote air trapping.

Albuterol is a β2-adrenergic agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle. A poor response in this case does not convert the process into restriction or identify a single cause of death from spirometry. Use the case to connect airway mechanism, expected obstructive measurements and the limitation of the available evidence.
keyPoints: Asthma: variable airflow obstruction
Albuterol: β2-mediated bronchodilation
Do not infer unprovided measurements or cause of death

questions.question: Which direct drug effect explains why albuterol was prescribed in the source case?

reasons: Surfactant inhibition would impair alveolar stability and is not albuterol action.
Albuterol stimulates β2 receptors and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle.
Oxidation causes methemoglobin and is not its therapeutic mechanism.
Pulmonary capillary closure is not the intended bronchodilator effect.

questions.question: Which finding would be most consistent with an obstructive pattern in this patient?
options: Reduced TLC is the only possible change
Increased hemoglobin concentration proves airway obstruction
FEV1 falls more than FVC, lowering the ratio
reasons: Reduced TLC defines restriction; obstruction may instead cause air trapping and normal/increased TLC.
Hemoglobin concentration concerns oxygen content, not expiratory airway mechanics.
Disproportionately reduced first-second volume is a typical obstructive pattern.
Effort and recording quality must be assessed before interpreting any pattern.

modules.title: Genomic DNA isolation & quantitation
modules.summary: Buccal cell collection, silica binding, reagent roles, washing/elution and NanoDrop interpretation from your MOL lab handout.

topics.title: Choose a DNA source and extraction method
body: Buccal cells are a painless, accessible source of genomic DNA. DNA is mainly nuclear, with a smaller mitochondrial component. The handout lists whole blood, tissues, saliva, cheek swabs and other biological material as potential sources; quantity and contamination differ with sample type.

The listed extraction approaches are organic phenol–chloroform, nonorganic proteinase K/salting out and silica-based extraction. This lab uses silica columns: lyse cells, bind DNA, wash contaminants away, then elute. Concentration and purity determine whether an extract is suitable for later PCR or restriction digestion.
keyPoints: This lab: buccal cells + silica column
Sequence: lyse → bind → wash → elute
DNA quantity and purity answer different questions

questions.question: What is the correct conceptual order of the silica extraction used in this MOL lab?
reasons: Elution comes after DNA has been released, bound and washed.
Washing an unbound sample cannot implement the column purification sequence.
DNA must first be released from cells; elution is the final recovery step.
Lysis releases DNA, binding retains it on silica, washing removes contaminants and elution recovers it.
questions.explanation: Lysis releases DNA, binding retains it on silica, washing removes contaminants and elution recovers it.

questions.question: Why measure both concentration and purity before using extracted DNA?
options: A sample can have a high DNA quantity but still contain interfering contaminants
Purity and concentration are identical values
A260/A280 directly gives total DNA mass
All buccal samples contain the same DNA yield
reasons: Amount alone does not show whether protein, salts or other contaminants may interfere with downstream use.
Concentration is amount per volume; purity ratios describe absorbance relationships.
Total mass requires concentration multiplied by recovered volume.
The handout gives a yield range, reflecting variation among samples.
questions.explanation: Amount alone does not show whether protein, salts or other contaminants may interfere with downstream use.

topics.title: Explain each reagent by its purpose
body: PBS suspends/preserves collected cells before lysis. Proteinase K digests proteins, including proteins associated with DNA. Lysis solution C disrupts cellular and nuclear membranes. Chaotropic salts destabilize proteins and help nucleic acids bind silica under the specified conditions.

Absolute ethanol enhances nucleic-acid binding to silica. The pre-wash removes protein/degraded-RNA residues; the wash removes residual salts. A low-salt elution buffer rehydrates DNA and reduces its affinity for silica so it is recovered into a clean tube. Reagents are not interchangeable: adding elution buffer at the binding stage would undermine the intended chemistry.
keyPoints: Proteinase K: protein digestion
Chaotropic salts + ethanol: binding conditions
Low salt: elution

questions.question: Which reagent is a peptidase that helps remove proteins during DNA isolation?
reasons: PBS is a buffered salt solution for handling cells, not a protease.
Proteinase K cleaves peptide bonds and helps digest protein material.
Elution buffer releases DNA from silica under low-salt conditions.
Silica is the binding surface rather than a protein-digesting enzyme.
questions.explanation: Proteinase K cleaves peptide bonds and helps digest protein material.

questions.question: Why is ethanol added before loading the silica column?
options: It is used to measure protein at 280 nm
It replaces the need for cell lysis
It enhances binding of nucleic acids to silica
It is the final low-salt elution reagent
reasons: Optical measurement is a later step and does not explain ethanol addition.
Cell lysis is still needed to release DNA before column loading.
The handout specifies ethanol to promote nucleic-acid binding under the extraction conditions.
Ethanol-containing binding/washing conditions differ from the final low-salt elution step.
questions.explanation: The handout specifies ethanol to promote nucleic-acid binding under the extraction conditions.

questions.question: Follow the DNA to the silica surface in the figure. What should stay on that surface during the wash?
options: All liquid that passed into the collection tube
Only proteins from the original lysate
reasons: The binding conditions retain nucleic acid while the wash removes soluble contaminants.
The flow-through is physically separate from the retained material.
The isolation is designed to enrich DNA rather than retain protein.
questions.explanation: The binding conditions retain nucleic acid while the wash removes soluble contaminants.

topics.title: Prepare the buccal sample and lysate
body: The supplied protocol specifies no food or drink in the preceding30 minutes; scrape each inner cheek six times and air-dry the swab for at least2 hours. Place the swab in a2 mL tube with400 μL PBS. Add20 μL proteinase K and400 μL lysis C, then vortex immediately for 15 seconds.

Incubate at 56 °C for 10 minutes, briefly centrifuge at 8000rpm for 1 minute to collect lid droplets, then add400 μL absolute ethanol, mix and briefly spin again. These volumes, temperatures and rpm are the handout’s specific protocol; do not generalize rpm to another rotor as an equivalent force.
keyPoints: PBS400 μL; proteinase K20 μL; lysis C400 μL
56 °C for 10 minutes
Then400 μL ethanol

questions.question: Which incubation matches this specific handout after lysis solution and proteinase K are added?
reasons: The extraction procedure gives56 °C for 10 minutes before the ethanol addition.
This is not the stated lysis incubation and can damage or alter the sample.
The protocol does not specify an overnight room-temperature incubation here.
A brief cold step is not the specified proteinase/lysis incubation.
questions.explanation: The extraction procedure gives56 °C for 10 minutes before the ethanol addition.

questions.question: Before column loading, the nominal liquid additions are400 μL PBS,20 μL proteinase K,400 μL lysis C and400 μL ethanol. Total added volume?
reasons: 700 μL is one specified column loading portion, not the total added liquid.
820 μL is the total before ethanol addition.
150 μL is the later elution volume.
400+20+400+400=1220 μL, explaining why loading is performed in more than one portion.
questions.explanation: 400+20+400+400=1220 μL, explaining why loading is performed in more than one portion.

topics.title: Load, wash and dry the column
body: Load700 μL without wetting the spin-column rim, centrifuge at 8000rpm for 1 minute and discard the flow-through. Repeat with the remaining lysate. DNA remains on silica during this stage; the collection-tube liquid is not the desired final DNA extract.

Add500 μL pre-wash, spin at 8000rpm for 1 minute and discard flow-through. Add500 μL wash and spin at 13300rpm for 3 minutes. The recommended extra full-speed1 minute spin reduces wash-buffer carryover. Residual ethanol can interfere with downstream work, so drying is distinct from elution.
keyPoints: Binding/wash flow-through is discarded
Pre-wash500 μL then wash500 μL
Extra dry spin reduces carryover

questions.question: After the first binding spin, where should the retained DNA principally be?
options: On the outside of the column cap
reasons: The purpose of lysis and column loading is to release DNA and capture it on silica.
Under binding conditions DNA is retained on silica while much of the lysate passes through.
The flow-through is discarded because the intended DNA is on the column.
The outside of the cap is not the binding surface and wetting the rim should be avoided.
questions.explanation: Under binding conditions DNA is retained on silica while much of the lysate passes through.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the recommended additional full-speed dry spin after washing?
options: Raise the A260 reading by adding protein
Elute DNA into the original dirty collection tube
reasons: Protein contamination can distort absorbance; it is not a desired result.
Centrifugation does not convert RNA into DNA.
The extra spin removes remaining wash liquid, including ethanol-containing carryover.
Elution occurs later into a clean tube after elution buffer is added.
questions.explanation: The extra spin removes remaining wash liquid, including ethanol-containing carryover.

questions.question: In the assembled column image, where would you find material that has passed through the membrane?
options: In the tube beneath the column
Above the membrane in the upper reservoir
Within the closed cap above the assembly
reasons: The lower tube collects the flow-through after centrifugation.
That is the loading region before passage through the membrane.
The cap does not receive the flow-through.
questions.explanation: The lower tube collects the flow-through after centrifugation.

topics.title: Recover DNA and distinguish concentration from yield

references.locator: DNA extraction procedure step12; DNA Quantitation N.B.

body: Move the column into a clean1.5 mL tube and discard the used collection tube. Add150 μL elution buffer, incubate5 minutes at 15–25 °C, then spin at 8000rpm for 1 minute. This flow-through is now the desired DNA eluate, unlike the binding/washing flow-through.

The handout gives a typical buccal-swab yield of 0.5–3.5 μg in 150 μL, approximately3–23 ng/μL. Total mass=concentration×recovered volume:20 ng/μL×150 μL=3000 ng=3 μg. Its long-term storage note recommends Buffer AE at−30 to−15 °C.
keyPoints: Clean collection tube for elution
150 μL buffer;5 minutes; collect eluate
Yield is mass; concentration is mass/volume

questions.question: Which flow-through should be retained as the desired extract?
options: The first binding spin before washing
The final elution spin into a clean tube
reasons: Binding-stage flow-through is discarded while DNA remains on silica.
Pre-wash liquid carries removed contaminants and is discarded.
Wash liquid is discarded; retaining it would also retain unwanted wash components.
Low-salt elution releases DNA from silica into the clean collection tube.
questions.explanation: Low-salt elution releases DNA from silica into the clean collection tube.

references.locator: DNA extraction procedure step12; DNA Quantitation N.B.

questions.question: A150 μL eluate measures20 ng/μL. What total DNA mass was recovered?
reasons: 20×150=3000 ng, and1000 ng=1 μg, so the yield is3 μg.
20 ng/μL is a concentration; it does not become20 μg without multiplying and converting.
150 is the volume, not the DNA mass.
3000 ng is3 μg, not3000 μg; this distractor misses the unit conversion.
questions.explanation: 20×150=3000 ng, and1000 ng=1 μg, so the yield is3 μg.

references.locator: DNA extraction procedure step12; DNA Quantitation N.B.

activities.prompt: An eluate has10 ng/μL DNA in 150 μL. Enter total yield in μg.
activities.explanation: 10×150=1500 ng=1.5 μg. Use the recovered volume if it differs from the nominal elution volume.

topics.title: Blank and measure on the NanoDrop
body: Select Nucleic Acid → dsDNA. Clean both pedestals using2 μL deionized water, lower the arm to contact both surfaces, then wipe with a clean dry Kimwipe. Apply2 μL blanking solution, lower the arm and Blank, then clean both pedestals again.

Apply2 μL nucleic acid sample, lower the arm and Measure. The software reports concentration and purity ratios. Finish the experiment and clean both surfaces. Blank with the appropriate solution for the sample matrix; a contaminated pedestal or mismatched blank can distort the result.
keyPoints: Choose dsDNA
Clean → blank → clean → sample → measure
Use2 μL as specified in this handout

questions.question: Why should the instrument be blanked before measuring the DNA sample?
options: To bind DNA permanently to the pedestal
To account for absorbance from the blanking solution/background
To remove the need for cleaning
To transform A280 into DNA concentration
reasons: NanoDrop is an optical measurement, not a silica-binding step.
Blanking sets the optical reference so background solution absorbance is accounted for.
Cleaning remains necessary between blank and sample and after measurements.
A280 mainly informs protein-related absorbance; blanking does not convert wavelengths.
questions.explanation: Blanking sets the optical reference so background solution absorbance is accounted for.

questions.question: Which software selection is specified for this extracted genomic DNA?
reasons: Protein A280 uses a different analytical mode and does not match the handout’s DNA setting.
Cell counting is not the listed optical measurement.
The handout explicitly selects the Nucleic Acid tab and dsDNA.
Flow cytometry is a different technology and is not the NanoDrop mode.
questions.explanation: The handout explicitly selects the Nucleic Acid tab and dsDNA.

questions.question: Locate the exposed measurement surface in the image. Where is the small sample applied?
options: In an open collection tube under the machine
On the outside of the upper arm casing
reasons: The droplet sits on the pedestal so the closed arm can establish the measurement path.
The instrument measures the droplet on the pedestal directly.
The outer casing does not form the measurement path.

topics.title: Interpret A260/A280 without overclaiming

references.locator: Introduction; DNA Quantitation; typical yield note

body: Nucleic acids absorb strongly near 260nm, while protein aromatic residues contribute at 280nm. The handout expects an A260/A280 ratio of 1.7–1.8 for its buccal DNA extracts. A low ratio can suggest contamination but is not a complete chemical analysis.

A ratio alone does not measure yield, fragment length, sequence correctness or guaranteed PCR success. Concentration determines how much sample provides a requested DNA amount; purity ratios are supplementary quality indicators. Gel electrophoresis can compare a sample with standards and also reveal features not captured by a ratio.
keyPoints: A260: nucleic acids; A280: protein contribution
Handout target ratio:1.7–1.8
A good ratio does not prove complete DNA integrity

questions.question: A sample has A260=0.36 and A280=0.20. What is its ratio and how does it compare with the handout?
options: 1.8; within the handout’s stated purity range
reasons: The ratio is a division, not a sum, and absorbance sum is not DNA concentration.
0.36/0.20=1.8, not0.56; the readings do not indicate absent DNA.
A ratio within range does not prove integrity or guarantee downstream success.
0.36÷0.20=1.8, matching the handout’s1.7–1.8 target while leaving other quality checks separate.
questions.explanation: 0.36÷0.20=1.8, matching the handout’s1.7–1.8 target while leaving other quality checks separate.

references.locator: Introduction; DNA Quantitation; typical yield note

questions.question: Which conclusion cannot be established from A260/A280 alone?
options: The exact DNA sequence and fragment integrity
Whether the measured ratio lies in the handout range
The relationship between the two absorbances
Whether a measured ratio is lower than 1.7
reasons: Absorbance ratios cannot determine sequence or fragment integrity; other methods are needed.
A numerical ratio can be compared with the stated range.
The ratio directly describes A260 relative to A280.
A numerical value can be compared with1.7, although the cause of a low value requires interpretation.

modules.summary: Trace arterial branches, dominance, veins and nodal relationships on specimens and angiograms, then apply them to infarction and bypass anatomy.

topics.title: Orient the specimen and follow the grooves
body: Before naming a vessel, identify the surface. The sternocostal surface is largely right ventricle, with the left ventricle to the anatomical left and the apex pointing down and left. The diaphragmatic surface is inferior; the base is predominantly posterior left atrium. A photograph can be rotated, so the top of the screen is not a reliable anatomical landmark.

The coronary (atrioventricular, AV) sulcus separates atria from ventricles. The RCA travels in the right AV groove; the circumflex travels in the left AV groove. The anterior interventricular groove runs between the ventricles toward the apex and contains the LAD with the great cardiac vein. The posterior interventricular groove contains the PDA/PIA with the middle cardiac vein.

Use a three-step identification routine: name the groove, follow the vessel toward its origin or termination, then check an accompanying vessel. A structure descending toward the apex is not automatically the LAD: on the inferior surface it may be the PDA. The crux is the junction of the posterior AV and posterior interventricular grooves.
keyPoints: AV groove: atrium–ventricle boundary; IV groove: ventricle–ventricle boundary.
Anterior IV: LAD + great cardiac vein; posterior IV: PDA + middle cardiac vein.
Crux: posterior AV groove meets posterior IV groove.

questions.question: A vessel descends toward the apex in the ANTERIOR interventricular groove. Which artery is being followed?
reasons: The circumflex follows the left AV groove rather than the anterior IV groove.
The PDA is in the posterior IV groove on the diaphragmatic aspect.
The LAD follows the anterior IV groove toward the apex, supplying anterior ventricular and septal regions.
The right marginal artery follows the acute right margin and supplies the RV.
questions.explanation: The LAD follows the anterior IV groove toward the apex, supplying anterior ventricular and septal regions.

questions.question: At the crux of the heart, which two surface grooves meet?
options: Anterior IV and left AV grooves
Posterior IV and posterior AV grooves
Right margin and anterior IV groove
reasons: The anterior IV groove is on the anterior surface, whereas the crux is posterior.
The crux is where the posterior interventricular groove meets the posterior atrioventricular groove.
An interatrial groove does not form the defined crux with the anterior IV groove.
The acute margin is not the junction used to define the crux.
questions.explanation: The crux is where the posterior interventricular groove meets the posterior atrioventricular groove.

questions.question: In this anterior specimen, which landmark best helps distinguish the RCA from the LAD?
options: Both run inside the ventricular cavities
The RCA crosses the apex, while the LAD stays in the AV groove
The RCA follows the right AV groove, while the LAD follows the anterior IV groove
reasons: Coronary arteries run on the external surface before giving myocardial branches, not within cavity lumina.
This reverses their main courses: the LAD heads toward the apex; the RCA follows the right AV groove.
Both coronary arteries carry systemic arterial blood; oxygen content does not distinguish them here.
Anatomical course is reliable: RCA in right AV groove; LAD in anterior IV groove.
questions.explanation: Anatomical course is reliable: RCA in right AV groove; LAD in anterior IV groove.

topics.title: Trace the RCA and its branches
body: The right coronary artery originates from the right coronary aortic sinus, just above the aortic valve. It passes between the right atrial appendage and pulmonary trunk, enters the right AV groove and continues toward the inferior surface. The sinus is part of the aortic root; it is not the right atrial chamber or the pulmonary valve.

Identify the right (acute) marginal branch along the acute margin of the heart. It primarily supplies the RV free wall. Smaller atrial and ventricular branches supply the nearby right atrium and right ventricle. The SA nodal artery commonly arises proximally from the RCA, but this is variable; a left-sided SA nodal supply does not imply left coronary dominance.

In the usual right-dominant arrangement, the distal RCA reaches the crux and gives the AV nodal branch and posterior interventricular artery (PDA/PIA). The PDA descends in the posterior IV groove, supplying adjacent inferior ventricular myocardium and posterior one-third of the septum. Always establish dominance before assuming every PDA arises from the RCA.
keyPoints: RCA origin: right coronary aortic sinus.
Right acute marginal: RV free wall.
At the crux in right dominance: AV nodal branch and PDA.

questions.question: Where should a catheter engage to opacify the RCA?
options: Coronary sinus opening in the right atrium
Pulmonary trunk above the pulmonary valve
reasons: The RCA begins at its ostium in the right coronary aortic sinus.
The coronary sinus is a venous collector opening into the RA, not an arterial origin.
The pulmonary trunk receives RV ejection; the coronary arteries originate from the aorta.
The appendage is atrial tissue; the RCA ostium is in the aortic root.
questions.explanation: The RCA begins at its ostium in the right coronary aortic sinus.

questions.question: A vessel runs along the acute right border of the heart. Which myocardium is its characteristic territory?
reasons: Anterior septal supply is mainly from LAD septal perforators.
The left atrium is mainly supplied by branches of the left coronary system.
The right marginal artery follows the acute margin and supplies the RV free wall.
Pulmonary venous wall is not the characteristic territory of the right marginal artery.
questions.explanation: The right marginal artery follows the acute margin and supplies the RV free wall.

questions.question: In a right-dominant heart, a branch from the distal RCA descends in the posterior IV groove. Which region is especially associated with its septal branches?
reasons: The anterior two-thirds of IV septum is mainly LAD territory.
The PDA supplies the posterior one-third of the IV septum and adjacent inferior ventricular regions.
The PDA is an interventricular vessel and does not exclusively supply the whole interatrial septum.
The left auricle is not the PDA’s defining territory.
questions.explanation: The PDA supplies the posterior one-third of the IV septum and adjacent inferior ventricular regions.

questions.question: In the supplied RCA angiogram, the numbered structure 4 is identified in the source as the posterior interventricular artery. Which route should it follow?
options: Across the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk
Along the left AV groove only
Down the posterior IV groove toward the apex
reasons: The PDA is a coronary surface artery, not a ventricular outflow structure.
The left AV groove is the circumflex course.
The AV node is near the interatrial septum, but the PDA follows the posterior IV groove.
The posterior IV artery descends on the inferior/diaphragmatic surface toward the apex.

topics.title: Distinguish LAD, diagonals and circumflex
body: The left main coronary artery begins in the left coronary aortic sinus and passes for a short distance between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle. Its main terminal branches are the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) and circumflex (LCx). Trace a branch by its groove rather than its apparent direction on a rotated picture.

The LAD runs in the anterior IV groove toward the apex. Diagonal branches leave it across the anterolateral LV wall; septal perforators enter the interventricular septum. LAD territory includes anterior LV, apex and anterior two-thirds of the septum, including much of the ventricular bundle-branch system. A diagonal branch and a septal perforator differ in both direction and target.

The circumflex wraps leftward in the AV groove, supplying the left atrium and lateral/posterolateral LV. Its left (obtuse) marginal branches descend across the lateral LV. In left dominance it also gives the PDA. The lab’s left-coronary diagram says “left (acute) marginal”; use obtuse marginal for the left ventricular margin, reserving acute marginal for the right side.
keyPoints: LAD: anterior IV groove; diagonal: LV surface; septal perforator: into septum.
LCx: left AV groove; obtuse marginal: lateral LV.
Source terminology correction: left margin is obtuse, not acute.

questions.question: A short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle bifurcates. Which pair is expected?
reasons: The RCA has a separate aortic origin; its right marginal branch is not a left-main terminal pair.
The left main coronary artery divides into LAD and circumflex.
These are venous tributaries, not branches of the left main artery.
The caval veins return systemic venous blood to the RA and do not arise from the left main.
questions.explanation: The left main coronary artery divides into LAD and circumflex.

questions.question: An anterior septal infarct is associated with new bundle-branch block. Which LAD branches connect the vascular lesion to conduction injury?
reasons: Right marginal branches primarily supply the RV free wall, not the anterior septum.
Circumflex atrial branches supply left atrial tissue rather than the anterior ventricular septum.
Veins drain blood; they do not provide the LAD arterial supply to the septum.
LAD septal perforators supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum and much of the bundle-branch system.
questions.explanation: LAD septal perforators supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum and much of the bundle-branch system.

questions.question: The source diagram calls a circumflex branch “left (acute) marginal.” Which correction best matches standard anatomical usage and the supplied A6 lecture?
options: Left obtuse marginal: branch supplying lateral LV
Right obtuse marginal: branch supplying the RA only
Left septal perforator: branch running in the AV groove
Posterior IV vein: branch of the left main artery
reasons: The left ventricular margin is obtuse; obtuse marginal branches usually arise from LCx and supply lateral LV.
The acute marginal is right-sided; “right obtuse marginal” does not correct the left branch shown.
A septal perforator enters the septum rather than running along the left margin.
A vein cannot be a branch of the left main coronary artery.
questions.explanation: The left ventricular margin is obtuse; obtuse marginal branches usually arise from LCx and supply lateral LV.

questions.question: In this left-coronary angiogram, source label 9 marks the circumflex. Which relationship should support that identification?
options: It is the longest vein in the anterior IV groove
It arises from the right aortic sinus and follows the acute margin
It curves around the heart in the left AV groove
reasons: The great cardiac vein accompanies the LAD initially; label9 is an artery.
That describes the right coronary/right marginal system, not LCx.
The circumflex wraps in the left AV groove and gives marginal/posterolateral branches.
The membranous septum is intracardiac tissue, not an opacified coronary branch.
