topics.title: Determine dominance before assigning inferior territory
body: Coronary dominance is defined by the origin of the posterior interventricular artery (PDA/PIA), not by which main coronary artery is visually larger, which supplies the SA node, or which supplies more total myocardium. Right dominance means PDA from RCA; left dominance means PDA from circumflex. Codominant patterns share posterior/inferior supply, with definitions varying between anatomical descriptions.

On a specimen or angiogram, find the posterior IV groove, identify its artery, then trace it back to its parent. Do not decide dominance from an anterior photograph that does not show the PDA origin. A single fixed 3D specimen represents one arrangement; changing its color cannot create a different vascular variant.

The distinction matters clinically. The PDA supplies posterior septum and the dominant artery usually gives the AV nodal branch near the crux. Thus an RCA lesion can combine inferior infarction with AV nodal block in a right-dominant heart; in a left-dominant heart the corresponding risk can arise from a circumflex lesion. Territorial boundaries and percentages vary, so apply the stated anatomy rather than treating population averages as a guarantee.
keyPoints: Find PDA → trace parent → assign dominance.
SA nodal origin does not define dominance.
Inferior territory and AV nodal supply depend on the actual dominant system.

questions.question: The PDA arises from the circumflex, although the RCA looks large. What is the dominance?
options: Right, because RCA diameter determines dominance
Codominant, because both main coronary arteries exist
Left, because the circumflex gives the PDA
Indeterminate until the SA nodal artery is found
reasons: Size does not define dominance.
Both arteries normally exist in all dominance patterns; their existence does not establish codominance.
A PDA originating from circumflex establishes left dominance.
SA nodal origin is variable and does not define dominance.
questions.explanation: A PDA originating from circumflex establishes left dominance.

questions.question: An inferior infarct causes AV block in a LEFT-dominant circulation. Which parent vessel is particularly relevant?
reasons: In left dominance the circumflex supplies the PDA territory and usually the AV nodal branch.
Diagonals chiefly supply anterolateral LV, not the usual AV nodal territory at the crux.
The right marginal supplies RV free wall and does not account for dominant left-system AV nodal supply.
The great cardiac vein is venous drainage, not the arterial culprit.
questions.explanation: In left dominance the circumflex supplies the PDA territory and usually the AV nodal branch.

questions.question: The SA nodal artery comes from the circumflex. What can be concluded about dominance from this fact ALONE?
options: It proves absence of a PDA
Dominance still requires tracing the PDA origin
reasons: A left-sided SA nodal supply can occur without left coronary dominance.
The SA nodal artery does not establish right dominance either.
Nodal origin does not imply the PDA is absent.
The PDA origin, not SA nodal origin, defines dominance.
questions.explanation: The PDA origin, not SA nodal origin, defines dominance.

activities.prompt: Complete: Coronary dominance is defined by the origin of the ______ artery.
activities.explanation: Trace the posterior interventricular/posterior descending artery to RCA or circumflex.

topics.title: Follow cardiac veins into the coronary sinus
body: The coronary sinus is a large venous channel in the posterior AV groove. It receives most cardiac venous return and opens into the right atrium between the IVC opening and the tricuspid orifice. Do not confuse this venous sinus with the right and left aortic sinuses that contain coronary arterial ostia.

The great cardiac vein begins near the apex, ascends beside the LAD in the anterior IV groove, then turns into the left AV groove with the circumflex and continues into the coronary sinus. The middle cardiac vein ascends beside the PDA in the posterior IV groove. The small cardiac vein follows the right marginal region and right AV groove to the sinus.

The posterior vein of the LV drains posterior LV into the coronary sinus. The oblique vein of the LA is another tributary in A6, but the lecturer notes that these fine veins may be difficult to identify macroscopically. Your practical recognition targets are the coronary sinus and great, middle and small veins; explain smaller tributaries without pretending every specimen will display them clearly.
keyPoints: Great vein + LAD; middle vein + PDA; small vein + right marginal/RCA.
Coronary sinus: posterior AV groove → right atrium.
Aortic sinuses give arteries; coronary sinus receives veins.

questions.question: A vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery and ascends from the apex. Which vein is it?
reasons: The great cardiac vein initially accompanies the LAD in the anterior IV groove.
The middle cardiac vein follows the PDA in the posterior IV groove and drains into the sinus.
The oblique vein lies on the left atrium, not along the posterior IV groove.
Anterior cardiac veins cross the right AV groove and drain directly into RA.
questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein follows the PDA in the posterior IV groove and drains into the sinus.

questions.question: A large venous channel lies in the posterior AV groove. Where does it terminate?
options: Left ventricle through the aortic valve
Left atrium through a pulmonary vein
reasons: The coronary sinus does not empty through the LV outflow or aortic valve.
Pulmonary veins return to LA, but the coronary sinus ends in RA.
The pulmonary trunk is an arterial RV outflow vessel.
The coronary sinus opens into the RA, collecting most cardiac venous return.
questions.explanation: The coronary sinus opens into the RA, collecting most cardiac venous return.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly traces the great cardiac vein?
options: Apex → anterior IV groove beside LAD → left AV groove → coronary sinus
Apex → posterior IV groove beside PDA → aorta
Right marginal artery → left atrial appendage → pulmonary vein
reasons: The great cardiac vein ascends beside LAD, turns into left AV groove and continues into the sinus.
This mixes systemic venous inflow with RV outflow and omits the great cardiac vein.
The posterior IV companion is the middle cardiac vein, which drains to the sinus rather than aorta.
The right marginal companion is the small cardiac vein; it does not drain to a pulmonary vein.
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein ascends beside LAD, turns into left AV groove and continues into the sinus.

questions.question: In this posterior view, which landmark helps distinguish the coronary sinus from a vein descending between the ventricles?
options: It runs transversely in the posterior atrioventricular groove
It tracks the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex
It lies entirely inside the ventricular blood pool
reasons: The coronary sinus follows the posterior atrioventricular boundary.
This is the characteristic initial course of the great cardiac vein.
The coronary sinus is a surface collecting vein.
questions.explanation: The coronary sinus follows the posterior atrioventricular boundary.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering

activities.prompt: Match the venous structure with its companion or destination.

figure.caption: Posterior venous view: locate the coronary sinus in the posterior atrioventricular groove.

topics.title: Recognize veins that bypass the coronary sinus
body: The statement “all cardiac veins drain through the coronary sinus” is an overgeneralization. Most do; two important direct routes bypass it. Anterior cardiac veins arise on the anterior RV, cross the right AV groove and enter the right atrium separately.

The smallest cardiac veins (venae cordis minimae, or Thebesian veins) are minute intramyocardial channels that open directly into chambers. They are not major named surface veins to hunt for with the naked eye. Keep them distinct from the Thebesian valve, which guards the coronary-sinus opening.

For a practical answer, give both origin and termination: anterior RV → anterior cardiac veins → RA directly. Great/middle/small cardiac veins → coronary sinus → RA is a different route, even though both ultimately reach the same atrium.
keyPoints: Anterior cardiac veins: RV surface → RA directly.
Smallest/Thebesian veins: microscopic channels → chambers directly.
Thebesian veins and Thebesian valve are different structures.

questions.question: Which veins cross the right AV groove and open directly into the RA rather than entering the coronary sinus?
reasons: The great cardiac vein enters/continues into the coronary sinus.
The middle cardiac vein is a coronary-sinus tributary.
Anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior RV directly into the RA.
The posterior LV vein generally opens into the coronary sinus.
questions.explanation: Anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior RV directly into the RA.

questions.question: Which description best identifies the smallest cardiac veins?
options: Microscopic channels opening directly into cardiac chambers
Large venous trunk in the posterior AV groove
A valve guarding the IVC orifice
An arterial branch to the AV node
reasons: Venae cordis minimae are tiny intramyocardial channels opening directly into chambers.
That is the coronary sinus.
The IVC valve is Eustachian; this is not a vein network.
The AV nodal artery provides arterial supply, not direct venous drainage.
questions.explanation: Venae cordis minimae are tiny intramyocardial channels opening directly into chambers.

topics.title: Locate nodes and trace the ventricular conduction pathway
body: The SA node lies subepicardially at the SVC–RA junction, near the upper end of the crista terminalis and corresponding external sulcus terminalis. It is not a grossly obvious colored bead in a dissection. Use its relationship to landmarks rather than claiming that ordinary myocardium can be distinguished visually as nodal tissue.

The AV node lies in the inferior interatrial septal region, superior and medial to the coronary-sinus opening, near the septal tricuspid cusp. A6 discusses Koch’s triangle but explicitly accepts the simpler coronary-sinus/tricuspid relationship. The AV nodal artery usually comes from the dominant coronary artery near the crux. SA nodal supply is more variable and usually comes from RCA, sometimes the left coronary system.

The AV bundle (His) passes through the fibrous skeleton near the membranous IV septum and divides into right and left bundle branches along the septum. Subendocardial Purkinje fibers distribute activation. The RV moderator band carries right-bundle fibers toward the anterior papillary muscle. Nodes and fibers are specialized cardiac cells, not peripheral nerves; a surface artery model cannot display them unless those tissues were actually segmented.
keyPoints: SA node: subepicardial SVC–RA junction, upper crista terminalis.
AV node: above/medial to coronary-sinus opening near septal tricuspid cusp.
His crosses fibrous skeleton; moderator band carries right-bundle fibers.

questions.question: Which relationship locates the SA node most accurately?
options: SVC–RA junction near upper crista terminalis, subepicardial
Posterior IV groove at the apex
reasons: The LV apex receives distal ventricular conduction, not the primary SA pacemaker.
The SA node lies subepicardially at the SVC–RA junction near the upper crista terminalis.
The posterior IV groove contains PDA and middle cardiac vein, not SA node.
The left auricle is not the normal SA nodal location.
questions.explanation: The SA node lies subepicardially at the SVC–RA junction near the upper crista terminalis.

questions.question: During a right atrial dissection, which region is closest to the AV node?
options: Above and medial to the coronary-sinus opening near the septal tricuspid cusp
At the opening of the left superior pulmonary vein
reasons: This inferior interatrial septal relationship identifies the AV nodal region.
Pulmonary veins open into LA, away from the AV nodal region described.
The acute margin relates to RV and right marginal vessels.
The anterior IV groove contains LAD/great cardiac vein, not AV node.
questions.explanation: This inferior interatrial septal relationship identifies the AV nodal region.

questions.question: Which conduction structure normally crosses the fibrous insulating plane between atrial and ventricular myocardium?
reasons: The SA node initiates atrial activation and does not pierce the fibrous plane into ventricles.
The great cardiac vein is venous drainage.
The moderator band carries part of the right bundle within RV after the His pathway has crossed.
The AV bundle traverses the fibrous skeleton, providing the normal conducting connection.
questions.explanation: The AV bundle traverses the fibrous skeleton, providing the normal conducting connection.

questions.question: An RV muscular bridge runs from septum to the anterior papillary muscle. What does it carry?
options: Part of the right bundle branch
reasons: The left coronary main stem is extracardiac at the aortic root.
The great cardiac vein runs on the anterior surface, not through this bridge.
The moderator band/septomarginal trabecula carries right-bundle fibers to the anterior papillary muscle/free wall.
Pulmonary venous blood enters LA, not an RV myocardial bridge.
questions.explanation: The moderator band/septomarginal trabecula carries right-bundle fibers to the anterior papillary muscle/free wall.

activities.prompt: Complete: The AV bundle passes close to the ______ part of the interventricular septum.
activities.explanation: The AV bundle crosses the fibrous skeleton near the membranous septum, explaining surgical vulnerability in that region.

topics.title: Apply vascular territories to infarction and block
body: Territories are useful anatomical predictions, not perfectly sharp borders. LAD supplies anterior LV, apex and anterior two-thirds of the septum through septal branches; diagonals supply anterolateral LV. LCx supplies lateral/posterolateral LV and left atrium. RCA supplies RA and most RV; in right dominance its distal branches also supply inferior ventricular and posterior septal regions.

Link a conduction disturbance to its tissue supply. Anterior septal infarction after proximal LAD occlusion may damage ventricular bundle branches. Inferior infarction with AV nodal block suggests injury to the dominant artery’s AV nodal branch near the crux. The same clinical pattern can arise from different parent arteries when dominance changes.

Lesion level matters. A proximal left-main lesion threatens both LAD and circumflex territories; a distal diagonal lesion does not eliminate flow through every left-coronary branch. In a left-dominant heart, a proximal left-main obstruction also threatens posterior septal supply through LCx/PDA. State the anatomy provided in the scenario before assigning the culprit.
keyPoints: Anterior septal injury → consider LAD septal perforators and bundle branches.
Inferior MI + AV block → consider dominant artery / AV nodal supply.
Proximal lesions generally threaten more downstream territory than distal branch lesions.

questions.question: A proximal LAD occlusion produces anterior septal infarction. Which additional finding is anatomically plausible?
options: Isolated failure of pulmonary venous drainage
New bundle-branch block from septal conduction ischemia
Selective loss of the right atrial auricle only
reasons: Pulmonary venous drainage is not the direct arterial territory affected by LAD.
LAD septal perforators supply much of the bundle-branch system; ischemia can disturb ventricular conduction.
Arterial occlusion does not remove all cardiac venous channels.
LAD primarily threatens anterior LV/apex/septum rather than selectively the RA auricle.
questions.explanation: LAD septal perforators supply much of the bundle-branch system; ischemia can disturb ventricular conduction.

questions.question: A right-dominant patient has inferior MI and new AV block. Which explanation is best?
options: RCA ischemia can involve the AV nodal branch near the crux
The great cardiac vein directly depolarizes the AV node
The SA nodal artery always arises from LAD
The circumflex never supplies conduction tissue
reasons: In right dominance the distal RCA usually gives the AV nodal artery, linking inferior MI and nodal block.
Veins return blood and are not the normal conducting route into the AV node.
SA nodal origin is variable and is not always from LAD.
The left system can supply nodes and conduction tissue; “never” is false.
questions.explanation: In right dominance the distal RCA usually gives the AV nodal artery, linking inferior MI and nodal block.

questions.question: Compared with an isolated distal diagonal obstruction, a proximal left-main obstruction generally threatens more myocardium because it is upstream of which branches?
options: Only the posterior vein of LV
reasons: A vein is not a downstream arterial branch of the left main.
The right marginal comes from RCA, not left main.
Left main is upstream of LAD and circumflex, so both territories may lose supply.
The posterior LV vein drains blood and is not a left-main arterial branch.
questions.explanation: Left main is upstream of LAD and circumflex, so both territories may lose supply.

topics.title: Interpret stenosis and explain the bypass route
body: Coronary angiography outlines the lumen by injecting contrast through a catheter engaged at a coronary ostium. A narrowing is a stenosis; the visible contrast channel is not the same thing as the full thickness of the arterial wall. On the supplied angiograms, use the labeled branch courses and projection rather than memorizing a branch’s screen position.

Angioplasty expands a narrowed segment with a balloon; a stent is a scaffold left within the lumen to maintain patency. CABG instead creates an alternative route around the lesion, delivering blood to a coronary segment distal to the obstruction. A graft attached only upstream would not bypass the blocked segment.

The lab names internal thoracic artery and great saphenous vein as common conduits; the A6 lecture also mentions radial artery. A classic internal thoracic graft supplies LAD. Keep donor conduit, target coronary artery and stenosis location separate when explaining a diagram. This is anatomical understanding, not a recommendation for a particular patient’s treatment.
keyPoints: Angiogram: contrast-filled arterial lumen.
Balloon/stent: treat the narrowed lumen; CABG: route around obstruction.
Graft target must lie distal to the obstructing lesion.

questions.question: Where must the downstream end of a bypass graft be connected to bypass a coronary stenosis?
options: Into the target coronary artery distal to the obstruction
Into the RA chamber, upstream of the tricuspid valve
Only proximal to the obstruction with no distal connection
reasons: The coronary sinus drains myocardium and would not provide a coronary arterial bypass target.
A distal coronary connection supplies myocardium beyond the obstructed segment.
RA connection delivers venous chamber flow, not a systemic arterial route beyond the lesion.
An entirely proximal connection leaves the obstruction between graft flow and downstream myocardium.
questions.explanation: A distal coronary connection supplies myocardium beyond the obstructed segment.

questions.question: Which pair of vessels is specifically named as common CABG conduits in the supplied coronary lab?
options: Coronary sinus and great cardiac vein
Internal thoracic artery and great saphenous vein
reasons: The caval veins are major systemic venous trunks, not the named routine harvest conduits.
These pulmonary vessels are not the named graft conduits.
These drain the heart and are not the named common bypass conduits.
The lab explicitly identifies internal thoracic artery and great saphenous vein as common conduits.
questions.explanation: The lab explicitly identifies internal thoracic artery and great saphenous vein as common conduits.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes a stent from CABG?
options: A stent is a scaffold within a treated arterial lumen; CABG provides an alternative route past the lesion
A stent drains directly into RA; CABG closes the coronary ostium
Both require the coronary sinus to become the LAD
A stent is the same structure as a papillary muscle
reasons: A stent maintains local lumen patency after PCI; a bypass graft routes blood around the obstruction.
A stent does not drain to RA, and CABG does not aim to close the coronary origin.
Neither procedure converts a venous sinus into LAD.
Papillary muscles are ventricular myocardium supporting AV valves, not vascular implants.
questions.explanation: A stent maintains local lumen patency after PCI; a bypass graft routes blood around the obstruction.

questions.question: Use the arrow marking the narrowed segment. Where should a bypass deliver blood relative to the narrowing?
options: Beyond the narrowing in the downstream coronary segment
Only upstream of the narrowed segment
reasons: This supplies the territory without forcing flow through the narrowed segment.
Flow to the downstream territory would still have to cross the obstruction.
That does not deliver arterial blood into the target coronary segment.
questions.explanation: This supplies the territory without forcing flow through the narrowed segment.

Angiographic stenosis marked by the source arrow; CABG must provide a route distal to the obstruction.

modules.title: Internal heart & valve-mechanics wet lab
modules.summary: Recognize opened-heart landmarks, AV supports and outflow anatomy, then connect structure to conduction and the cardiac cycle.
modules.sourceNote: Week 2 CVP Lab Guide also covers this practical. Its overlapping material is linked in the relevant topics.

topics.title: Orient an opened heart before naming a chamber
body: The supplied interactive PPT consists of unlabeled wet-specimen photographs. Slide1 is an introductory collage, slides2–9 show different views of opened cardiac tissue, and slide10 is blank. These photographs support recognition practice but do not contain a printed answer key for the pins. Do not infer a chamber or pin answer solely from the letter B.

Use several independent clues: relative wall thickness, trabecular texture, valve cusps and their chordae, and the connection to a great vessel. LV myocardium is approximately two to three times thicker than RV because it generates systemic pressure; the chamber lumen itself is not myocardium. Dissection can distort cavity shape, remove tissue and change apparent orientation.

At the bench, first find the apex and great-vessel roots, then trace an inlet through its valve to a ventricle and its outflow. The RV has rough inflow trabeculae and smooth infundibulum leading toward pulmonary valve. The LV leads through smooth aortic vestibule to aortic valve. Avoid calling every smooth surface an atrium or every cord a muscle.
Pause early in the supplied video: the probe and gloved hand rotate the intact specimen. Establish orientation before naming a cavity in a close-up.
keyPoints: Identify with relationships, not screen left/right or pin letter alone.
Wall thickness is a clue; confirm with valves and outflow.
A cavity is a space; myocardium forms its wall.

questions.question: An opened ventricle has a much thicker myocardial wall and an outflow into the aorta. Which chamber is it?
reasons: RA is a receiving atrial chamber and does not have the thick systemic ventricular wall.
RV ejects into pulmonary trunk and usually has a thinner wall than LV.
LA receives pulmonary veins and ejects across mitral valve, not directly into aorta.
LV has the thick systemic-pressure wall and aortic outflow.
questions.explanation: LV has the thick systemic-pressure wall and aortic outflow.

questions.question: A dissection photograph is rotated and deformed. Which approach gives the most defensible chamber identification?
options: Use only which side of the screen it occupies
Assume every large space is RA
Combine wall thickness, valve support and great-vessel continuity
Use pin B as a universal marker for LV
reasons: Screen position changes with rotation and is not an anatomical side marker.
Size alone is unreliable after dissection and does not define RA.
Independent anatomical relationships are more reliable than one visual clue.
Pin letters are local labels; the supplied PPT contains no universal B answer key.
questions.explanation: Independent anatomical relationships are more reliable than one visual clue.

questions.question: In a 3D heart model, a smooth surface is labeled “left ventricular cavity.” What does that surface represent?
options: The space occupied by blood, not the ventricular myocardium
reasons: A cavity segmentation represents the blood-containing space; the muscular wall is a different tissue.
Myocardium surrounds the cavity and must not be confused with the cavity surface.
The coronary artery supplies myocardium from its external course.
The pericardial sac surrounds the heart, not the LV blood space.
questions.explanation: A cavity segmentation represents the blood-containing space; the muscular wall is a different tissue.

topics.title: Recognize right atrial landmarks and fetal remnants
body: The right atrium receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus blood. Its smooth posterior sinus venarum is separated from the rough pectinate region by the crista terminalis internally. Pectinate muscles extend into the right auricle. The corresponding external groove is the sulcus terminalis.

The fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum marking the fetal foramen ovale. It is not a normally open adult hole. The Eustachian valve is the remnant at the IVC opening; the Thebesian valve guards the coronary-sinus opening. Neither is an AV valve with papillary muscles.

Connect chamber landmarks to conduction: the SA node is near the SVC opening at the upper crista terminalis; the AV nodal region is above/medial to the coronary-sinus opening near the septal tricuspid cusp. Ordinary dissection photographs do not make the microscopic nodal tissue directly identifiable.
keyPoints: Crista terminalis separates smooth sinus venarum from pectinate region.
Fossa ovalis: interatrial septal remnant of foramen ovale.
Eustachian: IVC; Thebesian valve: coronary sinus.

questions.question: Which structure separates the smooth sinus venarum from the pectinate region inside RA?
reasons: Moderator band is an RV bridge carrying right-bundle fibers.
Crista terminalis is the internal boundary between smooth and pectinate RA regions.
Aortic vestibule is smooth LV outflow.
A mitral leaflet lies between LA and LV, not within RA.
questions.explanation: Crista terminalis is the internal boundary between smooth and pectinate RA regions.

questions.question: A depression on the right side of the interatrial septum represents which fetal structure?
reasons: Ductus arteriosus becomes ligamentum arteriosum outside the chambers.
Ductus venosus becomes ligamentum venosum in the liver.
Left umbilical vein becomes ligamentum teres hepatis.
The fossa ovalis marks the former foramen ovale in the interatrial septum.
questions.explanation: The fossa ovalis marks the former foramen ovale in the interatrial septum.

questions.question: Which pairing is correct?
reasons: The Eustachian valve is at the IVC orifice in RA.
Thebesian valve guards coronary-sinus opening, not an aortic ostium.
Mitral valve guards the LA–LV orifice.
Pulmonary valve guards RV outflow into pulmonary trunk.
questions.explanation: The Eustachian valve is at the IVC orifice in RA.

activities.prompt: Match each right atrial landmark with its identity.

topics.title: Distinguish RV inflow, outflow and moderator band
body: The RV forms most of the anterior sternocostal surface. Its inflow region contains coarse trabeculae carneae and the tricuspid apparatus. Three tricuspid cusps—anterior, posterior and septal—are supported by chordae attached to papillary muscles. The septal cusp helps orient the valve relative to the interventricular septum.

The outflow region is the smooth infundibulum (conus arteriosus), leading to the pulmonary valve and pulmonary trunk. The rough inflow/smooth outflow distinction is more reliable than assuming the whole RV cavity has one texture. A muscular ridge or bridge must not be confused with a thin fibrous chorda.

The septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) crosses from the septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle/free wall. It carries part of the right bundle branch, helping coordinate activation. Its presence is an important RV landmark, but a severed or obscured band in one specimen cannot be taken as proof of its absence in normal anatomy.
keyPoints: RV inlet: trabeculae + tricuspid apparatus.
RV outlet: smooth infundibulum → pulmonary valve.
Moderator band: septum → anterior papillary muscle; right-bundle fibers.

questions.question: Which name identifies the smooth RV outflow tract?
reasons: Sinus venarum is the smooth receiving region of RA.
Aortic vestibule is the LV outflow tract.
Infundibulum/conus arteriosus is the smooth RV outflow leading to pulmonary valve.
Fossa ovalis is an atrial septal depression.
questions.explanation: Infundibulum/conus arteriosus is the smooth RV outflow leading to pulmonary valve.

questions.question: Which cusps belong to the tricuspid valve?
reasons: These are the aortic cusps, named by coronary relationships.
Tricuspid valve has anterior, posterior and septal cusps.
Two major anterior/posterior leaflets describe the mitral valve.
Anterior/right/left describes pulmonary cusps, not tricuspid.
questions.explanation: Tricuspid valve has anterior, posterior and septal cusps.

questions.question: Which feature best distinguishes a trabecula carnea from a chorda tendinea in a wet specimen?
options: Trabecula is a muscular ventricular ridge; chorda is a fibrous cord attaching an AV cusp
Both are arteries emerging from the aortic root
A chorda is always the thickest ventricular muscle
Trabeculae are found only in the atria
reasons: Trabeculae are myocardial ridges; chordae are fibrous cords linking AV cusps to muscular supports.
Neither structure is a coronary artery.
Chordae are fibrous cords, not the thick ventricular myocardium.
Atrial ridges are pectinate muscles; ventricular ridges are trabeculae carneae.
questions.explanation: Trabeculae are myocardial ridges; chordae are fibrous cords linking AV cusps to muscular supports.

figure.caption: Cropped ventricular wall with muscular ridges and adjoining chordae; distinguish myocardium from fibrous cords.

topics.title: Identify left atrium, LV and aortic vestibule
body: The LA forms most of the posterior base and usually receives four pulmonary veins. Its main wall is smooth, while pectinate muscles are chiefly in the left auricle. Blood exits through the mitral valve into LV. Pulmonary veins are venous because they carry blood toward the heart, despite being oxygenated.

The LV forms the apex and most of the left border, with a much thicker myocardial wall than RV. Mitral valve has anterior and posterior leaflets. Two principal papillary-muscle groups, anterolateral and posteromedial, each send chordae to both leaflets; do not assign one muscle exclusively to one leaflet.

The aortic vestibule is smooth LV outflow leading to the aortic valve. Contrast it with the trabeculated ventricular inlet and the RV infundibulum. Just above the aortic valve are the right and left coronary ostia. A cut open vessel must be traced before labeling it aorta or pulmonary trunk.
keyPoints: LA: posterior base, pulmonary veins, mainly smooth wall.
LV: apex, thick wall, mitral apparatus with two papillary groups.
Aortic vestibule: LV outflow; infundibulum: RV outflow.

questions.question: Which chamber usually receives four pulmonary veins?
reasons: RV ejects into pulmonary trunk; it does not receive pulmonary veins.
RA receives systemic veins and coronary sinus.
LV receives LA flow through mitral valve.
Four pulmonary veins usually enter the smooth posterior LA.
questions.explanation: Four pulmonary veins usually enter the smooth posterior LA.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes LV papillary-muscle support?
options: Each papillary muscle sends chordae only to one mitral leaflet
The two papillary groups send chordae to both mitral leaflets
LV papillary muscles support the aortic cusps
The mitral valve has no chordae
reasons: Each group supports both leaflets rather than one exclusive leaflet.
Anterolateral and posteromedial groups each send chordae to both mitral leaflets.
Aortic cusps have no papillary/chordal attachments.
Mitral is an AV valve supported by chordae and papillary muscles.
questions.explanation: Anterolateral and posteromedial groups each send chordae to both mitral leaflets.

questions.question: A smooth ventricular outflow leads directly to the aortic valve. Which structure is it?
reasons: The smooth LV outflow is the aortic vestibule.
Sinus venarum is the smooth posterior RA inflow.
Infundibulum leads from RV to pulmonary valve, not aortic valve.
The auricle is an atrial appendage, not a ventricular outflow.
questions.explanation: The smooth LV outflow is the aortic vestibule.

questions.question: Where are left atrial pectinate muscles mainly concentrated?
options: Throughout the smooth pulmonary venous wall
reasons: The main pulmonary venous portion of LA is smooth.
The aortic vestibule is LV outflow.
Pectinate muscles are mainly confined to the left auricle.
Pulmonary sinuses are related to semilunar cusps, not LA muscle ridges.
questions.explanation: Pectinate muscles are mainly confined to the left auricle.

topics.title: Trace leaflet → chordae → papillary muscle
body: Identify three different tissue components in the specimen: a thin flap is valve leaflet/cusp, narrow pale fibrous strands are chordae tendineae, and conical muscular projections are papillary muscles. Chordae attach the free edges and ventricular surfaces of AV leaflets to papillary muscle supports. Trabeculae carneae are muscular wall ridges rather than fibrous cords.

AV valves open and close passively with pressure differences. When atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, the valve opens for filling. As ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure in systole, the cusps close. Papillary muscles contract with the ventricle, tensioning chordae to prevent the closed cusps from prolapsing into the atrium; they do not pull the valve open.

Loss of a papillary/chordal support can allow systolic prolapse and regurgitation into the atrium. Keep this mechanical support function distinct from driving forward ejection: ventricular myocardium generates pressure, and valve opening depends on the gradient. In an image, do not label a cord “Purkinje fiber” simply because it looks pale; most conduction fibers are not grossly visible cords.
Use the close-up sequence to trace a fibrous cord from leaflet toward ventricular muscle. Compare those thin cords with the broader trabeculations in the wall.
keyPoints: Leaflet = flap; chorda = fibrous cord; papillary muscle = muscular projection.
Pressure closes AV valves; papillary/chordal tension prevents prolapse.
Semilunar cusps do not have chordae.

questions.question: In the specimen crop, which structure is represented by the thin pale strands running from muscle toward valve tissue?
reasons: Chordae are fibrous strands connecting AV valve tissue with papillary-muscle supports.
Coronary arteries are vascular tubes on/in the myocardial wall, not the characteristic AV supporting cords shown.
Pectinate muscles are atrial myocardial ridges, not thin fibrous AV cords.
Aortic sinuses are root recesses behind semilunar cusps.
questions.explanation: Chordae are fibrous strands connecting AV valve tissue with papillary-muscle supports.

figure.caption: Cropped opened ventricular inlet: thin valve tissue, fibrous chordae and muscular supports. The specimen is deformed by dissection.

questions.question: What is the main role of papillary-muscle contraction during ventricular systole?
options: Pull AV leaflets apart to initiate filling
Push blood directly through the coronary sinus
Tension chordae to prevent AV cusp prolapse into atria
reasons: Filling occurs in diastole; AV opening is pressure-driven, not pulled open by papillary muscles.
The coronary sinus drains into RA and is not emptied by papillary-muscle action.
Papillary contraction tensions chordae and prevents eversion/prolapse of closed AV leaflets.
Semilunar valves have no chordae or papillary attachments.
questions.explanation: Papillary contraction tensions chordae and prevents eversion/prolapse of closed AV leaflets.

questions.question: An AV valve’s chordae rupture. Which immediate mechanical problem becomes more likely in systole?
options: The valve becomes a new SA node
The leaflet can prolapse toward the atrium, permitting regurgitation
The coronary sinus becomes an artery
reasons: Chordae are mechanical supports and cannot become pacemaker tissue.
Loss of support permits leaflet prolapse and backward flow when ventricular pressure is high.
Rupture of valve cords does not transform venous anatomy.
Chordal rupture does not directly obstruct every pulmonary vein.
questions.explanation: Loss of support permits leaflet prolapse and backward flow when ventricular pressure is high.

questions.question: What directly opens an AV valve during ventricular filling?
options: Papillary muscles pulling cusps into the atrium
reasons: Papillary muscles prevent systolic prolapse, not open the AV valve into the atrium.
Valve motion is passive and pressure-driven; the leaflet is not an active pacemaker.
That gradient keeps the aortic valve closed and does not itself open the AV valve.
Atrial pressure greater than ventricular pressure drives AV valve opening and filling.
questions.explanation: Atrial pressure greater than ventricular pressure drives AV valve opening and filling.

activities.prompt: Complete: Papillary muscles tension the ______ to prevent AV cusp prolapse.
activities.explanation: Chordae transmit papillary-muscle tension to AV leaflets during ventricular systole.

figure.caption: Cropped opened ventricular inlet: thin valve tissue, fibrous chordae and muscular supports. The specimen is deformed by dissection.

topics.title: Recognize semilunar cusps and coronary ostia
body: Aortic and pulmonary valves each have three pocket-like cusps with central nodules. They lack chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. The pockets fill with a brief tendency to backflow when arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, bringing the cusp margins together.

The aortic cusps are right coronary, left coronary and posterior noncoronary. Coronary ostia lie in the right and left aortic sinuses above the corresponding cusps; the posterior sinus normally has no coronary ostium. The pulmonary cusps are anterior, right and left, and have no coronary ostia.

Opening and closure are pressure events: ventricular pressure above arterial pressure opens the semilunar valve; arterial pressure above ventricular pressure closes it. This applies to aortic/LV and pulmonary/RV relationships even though their pressure magnitudes differ. A preserved specimen shows structural relationships, not a live pressure-driven valve cycle.
keyPoints: Semilunar valves: three cusps, no chordae/papillary supports.
Aortic R/L coronary + posterior noncoronary; pulmonary anterior/right/left.
Coronary ostia are in aortic sinuses, not pulmonary sinuses.

questions.question: Which valve normally has no chordae tendineae?
reasons: Mitral leaflets have chordae attached to papillary muscles.
Tricuspid cusps have chordal support.
Aortic semilunar cusps close without chordae or papillary muscles.
Both AV valves normally possess chordae.
questions.explanation: Aortic semilunar cusps close without chordae or papillary muscles.

questions.question: Which aortic cusp/sinus is normally noncoronary in the orientation taught here?
reasons: Anterior is a pulmonary-cusp designation, not the noncoronary aortic cusp.
The posterior aortic cusp/sinus is the noncoronary one.
The right aortic sinus contains RCA ostium.
The left aortic sinus contains left coronary ostium.
questions.explanation: The posterior aortic cusp/sinus is the noncoronary one.

questions.question: What pressure relationship closes the aortic valve at the end of ejection?
reasons: This atrial comparison does not determine aortic-valve closure.
LV pressure above aortic pressure favors opening/ejection.
RA–RV gradient relates to tricuspid filling.
As LV pressure falls below aortic pressure, the reverse gradient fills the cusps and closes the aortic valve.
questions.explanation: As LV pressure falls below aortic pressure, the reverse gradient fills the cusps and closes the aortic valve.

activities.prompt: Match each valve to its supported anatomical description.

pairs.definition: Two AV leaflets with chordal support
Anterior, posterior and septal AV cusps
Right/left coronary and posterior noncoronary cusps
Anterior, right and left semilunar cusps

topics.title: Distinguish muscular septum, membranous septum and fibrous skeleton
body: The interventricular septum has a large thick muscular part and a small thin membranous part near the aortic valve and septal tricuspid cusp. The interatrial septum is a different partition and contains the fossa ovalis. Do not identify every thin septal flap as a ventricular septal defect.

The fibrous skeleton provides connective-tissue support around valve orifices, maintains their shape and anchors cusps and myocardium. It electrically separates atrial from ventricular myocardium. The normal AV bundle is the conducting route across this insulating plane.

The AV bundle runs near the lower border of the membranous IV septum before dividing. This proximity explains why repair in the perimembranous septal region can risk conduction injury. The gross photos do not resolve microscopic conduction fibers; learn the relationship from the A5 diagrams and use the 3D model only for structures actually segmented.
keyPoints: Most IV septum is muscular; membranous part is small and thin near aortic/septal tricuspid regions.
Fibrous skeleton: structural support + atrioventricular electrical insulation.
Perimembranous surgery can threaten the nearby AV bundle.

questions.question: Which relationship identifies the membranous IV septum?
options: Thin part near aortic valve and septal tricuspid cusp
Thick free wall at the LV apex
Pectinate region in the left auricle
reasons: The membranous IV septum is the small thin septal part near these valve landmarks.
The LV free wall is myocardial wall, not the membranous septum.
Pectinate atrial muscle is not an interventricular partition.
LA posterior wall is separate from the ventricular septum.
questions.explanation: The membranous IV septum is the small thin septal part near these valve landmarks.

questions.question: Why can perimembranous VSD repair cause conduction disturbance?
options: The SA node lies inside the LV apex
The coronary sinus is the normal atrioventricular conduction route
The AV bundle lies close to the membranous septal region
Papillary muscles normally conduct from SA to AV node
reasons: SA node is at SVC–RA junction, not LV apex.
The coronary sinus is venous; the AV bundle is the normal conducting connection.
The nearby AV bundle can be injured in the perimembranous region.
Papillary muscles receive ventricular activation but are not the SA-to-AV pathway.
questions.explanation: The nearby AV bundle can be injured in the perimembranous region.

questions.question: Which pair correctly describes the cardiac fibrous skeleton?
options: Valve-ring support and electrical insulation between atria and ventricles
Coronary venous pumping and SA-node generation
Opening semilunar cusps by active contraction
reasons: These are not the principal functions of dense cardiac fibrous rings.
The skeleton supports valve orifices and insulates atrial from ventricular muscle.
It is connective tissue rather than a pump or pacemaker.
It does not actively contract to open semilunar valves; gradients move the cusps.
questions.explanation: The skeleton supports valve orifices and insulates atrial from ventricular muscle.

topics.title: Link the specimen to valve states, sounds and volume
body: Use the existing 29-slide interactive cardiac-cycle source to animate your mental picture of the specimen. In ventricular filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure: AV valve open, semilunar valve closed, ventricular volume increasing. Near end-diastole, atrial contraction adds the atrial kick and volume reaches EDV.

Ventricular depolarization (QRS) precedes contraction. When ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, AV valves close and S1 occurs. During isovolumetric contraction both valve groups are closed, so pressure rises without a change in ventricular volume. Ejection starts only when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and the semilunar valve opens.

As ventricles relax, arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, closing semilunar valves and producing S2. The aortic trace shows a dicrotic notch. During isovolumetric relaxation both groups are closed and volume remains at ESV. AV opening follows when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure; rapid filling begins. Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV, not the full EDV.

Worked example (illustrative values, not measurements from this specimen): EDV120mL and ESV50mL yield SV70mL/beat. If volume remains at120mL while ventricular pressure rises and both valves are closed, the phase is isovolumetric contraction, not ejection. A static model can show structural position but cannot supply these pressures.
keyPoints: Filling: AV open, semilunar closed; ejection: reverse.
Both valve groups closed during both isovolumetric phases.
S1: AV closure; S2: semilunar closure; SV=EDV−ESV.

questions.question: LV pressure is rising, its volume remains at EDV, and both mitral and aortic valves are closed. Which phase is this?
reasons: Filling increases ventricular volume with the mitral valve open.
Ejection decreases ventricular volume and requires aortic opening.
Relaxation lowers pressure at ESV rather than raising it at EDV.
Both valves are closed while pressure rises at constant EDV during isovolumetric contraction.
questions.explanation: Both valves are closed while pressure rises at constant EDV during isovolumetric contraction.

questions.question: Illustrative EDV is120mL and ESV50mL. What is stroke volume?
reasons: Adding EDV and ESV gives170 but does not calculate ejected volume.
SV=EDV−ESV=120−50=70mL/beat.
EDV is the starting filled volume, not all of it is ejected.
ESV is the residual volume, not the ejected volume.
questions.explanation: SV=EDV−ESV=120−50=70mL/beat.

questions.question: Which event corresponds to S2 and the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation?
options: Opening of mitral and tricuspid valves
Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves
reasons: AV opening occurs after isovolumetric relaxation, when filling begins.
P wave precedes atrial contraction rather than defining S2.
Semilunar closure produces S2 as ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.
Papillary muscles do not attach to or open the aortic valve.
questions.explanation: Semilunar closure produces S2 as ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.

questions.question: After isovolumetric relaxation, what allows mitral opening and rapid LV filling?
options: LV pressure falls below LA pressure
Aortic pressure falls below RA pressure
LV pressure rises above aortic pressure
Chordae actively shorten to pull the valve open
reasons: The LA-to-LV pressure gradient opens the mitral valve and permits rapid filling.
This comparison does not govern the mitral orifice.
LV above aortic pressure favors aortic opening and ejection, not filling.
Chordae transmit passive support tension and do not actively open the valve.
questions.explanation: The LA-to-LV pressure gradient opens the mitral valve and permits rapid filling.

activities.prompt: Match each phase with its valve/volume state.

pairs.definition: Both closed; pressure rises at EDV
Both closed; pressure falls at ESV

modules.title: Thoracic skeleton and surface landmarks
modules.summary: Orient the sternum, ribs and thoracic vertebrae before identifying a labeled structure.

topics.title: Find the sternal angle and surface lines
body: Palpable steps in the sternum orient the cage.

The manubriosternal junction forms the sternal angle and identifies the second costal cartilage, giving a starting point for counting spaces. In drawings, distinguish the midclavicular and axillary reference lines from the actual bony margins.

questions.question: A marker is on the second costal cartilage at its sternal attachment. Which landmark is adjacent?
reasons: The second cartilage meets the sternum at the manubriosternal junction.
This is inferior near the xiphoid process.
It sits at the upper border of the manubrium.
questions.explanation: The second cartilage meets the sternum at the manubriosternal junction.

questions.question: Compare the vertical reference lines in the lateral view. Which line runs down from the apex of the axilla?
reasons: Its position aligns with the center of the axilla.
This line descends on the anterior chest from the clavicle.
This is a posterior landmark through the scapula.
questions.explanation: Its position aligns with the center of the axilla.

topics.title: Orient a typical rib and identify the first rib
body: Start posteriorly with head, neck and tubercle, then follow the shaft to the angle and anterior end.

The inferior internal groove accommodates the intercostal bundle. The short broad first rib has superior vascular grooves separated by the scalene tubercle. Distinguish the anterior vein groove from the more posterior arterial groove.

questions.question: Which structure separates the subclavian vessel grooves on the first rib?
reasons: Anterior scalene attaches at this landmark.
It is a change in shaft curvature rather than the divider of the superior grooves.
It is the inferior shaft groove for the intercostal bundle.
questions.explanation: Anterior scalene attaches at this landmark.

questions.question: Inspect the pair of shallow channels on either side of the raised first-rib landmark. Which channel is anterior to the scalene tubercle?
reasons: The vein passes anterior to anterior scalene and its tubercle.
The artery passes posterior to the tubercle.
This runs along the inferior internal aspect of a typical rib shaft.
questions.explanation: The vein passes anterior to anterior scalene and its tubercle.

topics.title: Explain the two posterior articulations
body: Identify a thoracic vertebra by facets for ribs.

In the typical pattern, the rib head meets adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervening disc, whereas the tubercle meets the transverse process at its own level. Orient the facet by where it sits, then account for atypical ribs with different articulation patterns.

questions.question: Which structure of a typical fifth rib meets the T5 transverse process?
reasons: The costotransverse joint is formed by the tubercle.
The head articulates with vertebral bodies and the disc in the typical pattern.
The anterior shaft approaches the costal cartilage.
questions.explanation: The costotransverse joint is formed by the tubercle.

questions.question: Follow the rib toward the vertebral column in this view. Which contact is farther lateral from the midline?
reasons: The transverse process projects laterally from the vertebral arch.
The body is medial to the transverse process.
The disc is near the midline between bodies.
questions.explanation: The transverse process projects laterally from the vertebral arch.

modules.title: External heart and pericardial sinuses
modules.summary: Read the surface and vessel roots before tracing the pericardial reflections.

topics.title: Orient the apex, base and surfaces
body: The apex points inferiorly and to the left and is formed by the left ventricle.
The base faces posteriorly and is mainly left atrial. The anterior surface is largely right ventricular. To orient an isolated heart, use chamber and vessel relationships as well as its outline.

questions.question: A broad surface receives four pulmonary veins. Which chamber contributes most of it?
reasons: Pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the posterior base.
It receives systemic venous return via venae cavae and coronary sinus.
It makes the apex and ejects into the aorta.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the posterior base.

activities.prompt: Match each structure to its identifying feature.

pairs.definition: Posterior surface mainly formed by left atrium

topics.title: Trace the pericardial reflections
body: Separate the transverse passage behind the arterial roots from the oblique recess behind the left atrium.
Reflections around aorta and pulmonary trunk mark the arterial boundary of the transverse sinus. Reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava bound the posterior recess.

questions.question: A probe passes behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk through a serous passage. Which sinus is shown?
reasons: It lies posterior to the arterial outflow roots.
It is the blind recess posterior to the left atrium.
It is a venous channel draining cardiac blood.
questions.explanation: It lies posterior to the arterial outflow roots.

questions.question: Trace the recess bounded by pulmonary venous reflections behind the atrium. Where would a probe following the recess end?
options: Across to the opposite side behind both arterial trunks
Within the right atrial blood pool
reasons: The oblique sinus is a cul-de-sac behind the left atrium.
That is the transverse sinus passage.
The recess is in the pericardial cavity rather than an intracardiac lumen.
questions.explanation: The oblique sinus is a cul-de-sac behind the left atrium.

modules.title: Cardiac wall and conduction histology
modules.summary: Identify three layers of the heart wall and distinguish conducting cells from contractile muscle.

topics.title: Read both surfaces of the cardiac wall
body: Find the chamber lumen and the outer surface before naming layers.

Endocardium lines the lumen and the exposed surface of papillary muscles. Epicardium is the visceral serous covering and has a mesothelial surface with variable subepicardial fat and neurovascular structures. The intervening myocardium is contractile.

questions.question: A mesothelial surface overlies adipose tissue and a coronary vessel. Which layer is shown?
reasons: Mesothelium plus subepicardial connective tissue identifies the outer layer.
This lines the blood-contacting chamber surface.
This is the contractile muscular middle layer.
questions.explanation: Mesothelium plus subepicardial connective tissue identifies the outer layer.

questions.question: Which visible combination in this micrograph locates the outer cardiac wall surface?
options: A thin surface lining over fat and loose connective tissue
A thin surface lining facing a chamber lumen with pale conduction cells underneath
A continuous thick band of branching muscle at the exposed edge
reasons: The epicardial mesothelium overlies subepicardial connective tissue.
That pattern supports ventricular endocardium.
Branching myocytes identify myocardium; the outer surface has a mesothelial lining.
questions.explanation: The epicardial mesothelium overlies subepicardial connective tissue.

topics.title: Identify myocardium in longitudinal section
body: Look for branching fibers, centrally placed nuclei and intercalated discs crossing cell boundaries.
Gap junctions support electrical coupling, while mechanical junctions link adjacent cells during contraction. A dark transverse junction differs from regular myofibrillar striation.

questions.question: Which feature most strongly supports cardiac rather than skeletal muscle in this field?
reasons: The discs connect individual cardiomyocytes.
Both skeletal and cardiac muscle can be striated.
Capillaries are present in both tissues.
questions.explanation: The discs connect individual cardiomyocytes.

questions.question: Compare the marked cell junctions with the finer recurring striations. What distinguishes the junctions in this field?
options: Dark transverse boundaries interrupting fibers at cell contacts
Regular pale spaces between every adjacent sarcomere
A long hollow channel containing erythrocytes
reasons: Intercalated discs occur at junctions between cardiomyocytes.
Sarcomere repetition is not a cell boundary.
That would suggest a vessel rather than an intercellular junction.
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs occur at junctions between cardiomyocytes.

topics.title: Locate Purkinje cells under endocardium
body: Scan the ventricular lining before looking for large pale cells just beneath it.

Purkinje fibers are glycogen-rich and have relatively sparse peripheral myofibrils. Distinguish them from deeper darker contractile cells and from empty fat spaces by location, nuclei and peripheral staining.

questions.question: Large pale nucleated cells just beneath ventricular endocardium have sparse peripheral myofibrils. What are they?
reasons: Their location and morphology identify specialized ventricular conduction cells.
These occur on the outer surface and have different vacuolated morphology.
These are slender connective tissue cells rather than large pale conducting myocytes.
questions.explanation: Their location and morphology identify specialized ventricular conduction cells.

questions.question: Compare the large pale cells near the lining with the darker muscle beneath. Which visible relationship supports identification as conduction fibers?
options: Pale nucleated cells clustered beneath the chamber lining
Empty rounded spaces in fat outside the muscle
Dark compact fibers forming the bulk of the wall
reasons: Subendocardial location and pale cytoplasm support Purkinje identification.
That describes subepicardial adipose tissue.
That is contractile myocardium.
questions.explanation: Subendocardial location and pale cytoplasm support Purkinje identification.

modules.title: Blood vessel microscopy
modules.summary: Classify vessels from the media, elastic laminae and outer layer.

topics.title: Compare elastic and muscular arteries
body: Find the lumen and compare media at the same magnification.

Multiple elastic sheets distributed across the media support an elastic artery. A muscular artery has a smooth-muscle-dominant media and a conspicuous inner elastic boundary. Follow that boundary around the lumen before naming a wavy feature.

questions.question: Which observation best identifies an elastic artery?
options: Repeated elastic lamellae across the media
A single prominent internal elastic lamina
Longitudinal muscle bundles mainly in adventitia
reasons: The repeated sheets contribute arterial stretch and recoil.
This feature commonly stands out in a muscular artery.
That pattern supports a large vein.
questions.explanation: The repeated sheets contribute arterial stretch and recoil.

questions.question: Look across the thick middle layer in the higher-power panel. Where is the elastic material distributed?
options: In repeated lamellae throughout the media
Only in a single sharply defined boundary
Only around vessels in the adventitia
reasons: This organization supports elastic recoil across the wall.
An isolated conspicuous elastic boundary is more characteristic of a muscular artery.
Outer-wall vessels do not account for the repeated medial sheets.
questions.explanation: This organization supports elastic recoil across the wall.

topics.title: Read the internal elastic lamina
body: In the muscular specimen, locate the intima at the lumen and the media immediately outside.
The internal elastic lamina sits at their junction and may appear scalloped. Use the stain and the neighboring muscle layers before judging whether a line represents tissue or a tear.

questions.question: Where should you look for the internal elastic lamina?
options: At the junction of intima and media
reasons: The sheet separates the intima from the underlying smooth muscle media.
That is external to the media and elastic boundary in question.
The lamina is part of the vessel wall.
questions.explanation: The sheet separates the intima from the underlying smooth muscle media.

questions.question: Use the image to distinguish the prominent wavy sheet from the tissue beneath it. What forms most of the adjacent media?
options: A stack of evenly repeated elastic sheets
reasons: The large smooth muscle media lies external to the internal elastic lamina.
That distribution would favor an elastic artery.
Fat does not form the media of this muscular artery.
questions.explanation: The large smooth muscle media lies external to the internal elastic lamina.

topics.title: Sort small vessels by wall and lumen
body: An arteriole has a small lumen encircled by a few smooth muscle layers.

A capillary is an endothelial tube without a continuous smooth muscle media. A postcapillary venule has a wider thin-walled profile. Compare more than one region because obliquity can make a wall look thicker.

questions.question: A tiny endothelial tube admits single-file red cells and lacks a continuous smooth muscle coat. Which profile is most consistent?
reasons: It has an endothelial exchange wall without a continuous media.
A smooth muscle coat should be visible around the lumen.
It has a much thicker media and a larger layered wall.
questions.explanation: It has an endothelial exchange wall without a continuous media.

questions.question: Compare the small vessels in the paired images. Which visual clue identifies the arteriole even when lumen shape is distorted?
options: A continuous smooth muscle rim around a small lumen
The broadest lumen with the thinnest wall
A tube allowing only a single file of red cells and lacking a muscle rim
reasons: Wall organization helps distinguish the arteriole from an adjacent thin-walled venule.
That combination favors a venular profile.
A single-file lumen with no muscle rim favors a capillary.
questions.explanation: Wall organization helps distinguish the arteriole from an adjacent thin-walled venule.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering

topics.title: Identify a large vein from its externa
body: Orient the wall before comparing stains.

A large vein typically has a relatively thin media and thick externa. In specimens such as the IVC, longitudinal smooth muscle bundles may be conspicuous in the outer layer. Lumen collapse and sectioning alter shape, so compare tissue composition as well.

questions.question: Which feature supports a vena cava section over an aortic section?
options: Longitudinal smooth muscle in a thick adventitia
Many elastic sheets throughout a thick media
reasons: This is a characteristic large-vein wall pattern.
This is characteristic of a conducting artery.
Both vessels have an endothelial lumen.
questions.explanation: This is a characteristic large-vein wall pattern.

questions.question: Compare the thickness of the outer connective tissue to the middle layer. Which pattern supports the large vein in this image?
options: A conspicuous externa relative to the thinner media
A media packed with many elastic lamellae and little externa
An endothelial wall without surrounding supporting tissue
reasons: This relationship helps identify the large vein even if its lumen is distorted.
This favors an elastic artery.
This is closer to a capillary profile.
questions.explanation: This relationship helps identify the large vein even if its lumen is distorted.

modules.title: Mediastinum and great vessel relations
modules.summary: Use the transverse plane and trace nerves and veins in a specimen.

topics.title: Locate the mediastinal compartments
body: Use the sternal-angle plane toward T4–T5 to separate superior from inferior mediastinum.
In the lower compartment, pericardium and heart occupy the middle region. The area between sternum and pericardium is anterior, and the area behind pericardium extends toward the vertebral column.

questions.question: Which mediastinal subdivision contains the heart and pericardium?
reasons: The pericardial sac defines the middle inferior compartment.
This is between sternum and pericardium.
This contains structures behind the pericardium such as descending thoracic aorta and esophagus.
questions.explanation: The pericardial sac defines the middle inferior compartment.

questions.question: In the sagittal diagram, which space lies between the sternum and pericardium below the transverse plane?
reasons: The anterior division lies immediately behind the sternum and in front of the pericardium.
It contains the pericardium and heart.
The superior mediastinum is above the transverse thoracic plane.
questions.explanation: The anterior division lies immediately behind the sternum and in front of the pericardium.

topics.title: Trace phrenic, vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves
body: At the root of the lung, phrenic descends anteriorly and vagus passes posteriorly.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch near ligamentum arteriosum before ascending. Trace origins and turns to distinguish crossing nerves.

questions.question: Which nerve normally passes anterior to the lung root on its way toward the diaphragm?
reasons: It descends on the fibrous pericardium anterior to the root.
It passes posterior to the root.
It loops under the arch and ascends toward the larynx.
questions.explanation: It descends on the fibrous pericardium anterior to the root.

questions.question: Use the lung root as a reference. Which paired course distinguishes the two nerves in the illustrated view?
options: Both nerves loop beneath the arch before returning upward
reasons: The phrenic travels toward the diaphragm anterior to the root, while vagus passes behind it.
The vagus passes behind the root and the phrenic passes in front.
That turn describes the left recurrent laryngeal branch rather than both nerves.
questions.explanation: The phrenic travels toward the diaphragm anterior to the root, while vagus passes behind it.

topics.title: Follow posterior venous return
body: Trace the azygos vein up the right side and over the right root toward SVC.
Left-sided hemiazygos connections cross toward the azygos system. Use arch direction and connection to SVC to distinguish the azygos arch from arterial branches.

questions.question: A venous arch crosses above the right lung root and enters the SVC. Which vessel is shown?
reasons: Its arch joins the SVC above the root.
It is a lymphatic route toward the left venous angle.
It is an arterial structure arching toward the left.
questions.explanation: Its arch joins the SVC above the root.

questions.question: Follow the large right-sided venous arch from the posterior thorax. Which connection identifies it as the azygos arch?
options: It curves over the right lung root into the SVC
It empties into the left atrium via pulmonary veins
It curves to the left and continues as the descending thoracic aorta
reasons: This is the characteristic terminal connection of the azygos arch.
The azygos system returns systemic venous blood.
That describes an arterial path.
questions.explanation: This is the characteristic terminal connection of the azygos arch.

modules.title: Upper airway gross practical
modules.summary: Navigate nasal drainage, laryngeal cartilages and the tracheobronchial tree.

topics.title: Read the nasal conchae and drainage
body: Find the choana leading posteriorly to nasopharynx, then use conchae as roofs over the meatuses.
Middle meatus is the important drainage region for maxillary and frontal sinuses and anterior ethmoidal cells. The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.

questions.question: Where does the nasolacrimal duct normally open?
reasons: It delivers tears beneath the inferior concha.
This region receives drainage from several paranasal sinuses.
This receives the sphenoid sinus drainage.
questions.explanation: It delivers tears beneath the inferior concha.

questions.question: Follow the passage immediately beneath the middle concha. Which region are you tracing?
reasons: Each meatus lies beneath its corresponding concha.
It lies above and behind the superior concha.
It lies beneath the inferior concha.
questions.explanation: Each meatus lies beneath its corresponding concha.

topics.title: Link folds, cartilage and muscle action
body: Orient thyroid, cricoid and arytenoid cartilages, then trace the vocal folds to the arytenoids.
Posterior cricoarytenoid abducts the folds. Cricothyroid increases tension and is supplied by the external superior laryngeal nerve. Separate pitch changes from problems opening the glottis.

questions.question: Which muscle actively abducts the vocal folds?
reasons: Its pull rotates the arytenoids to open the glottis.
It lengthens and tenses the folds.
It contributes to adduction.
questions.explanation: Its pull rotates the arytenoids to open the glottis.

questions.question: Compare the shield-shaped cartilage with the ring-shaped cartilage just below it. Which forms the complete ring?
reasons: It is the complete ring at the lower larynx.
It is the shield-like framework above the cricoid.
The arytenoids are paired cartilages resting on the posterior cricoid.
questions.explanation: It is the complete ring at the lower larynx.

topics.title: Orient tracheal rings and main bronchi
body: Find the posterior gap in the C-shaped cartilage where trachealis lies adjacent to the esophagus.
The carina marks the bifurcation. The right main bronchus is typically wider and more vertical, which helps explain the tendency for aspirated material to enter it.

questions.question: Which feature identifies the posterior tracheal wall?
options: Open cartilage ends connected by trachealis
A ridge at every tracheal ring
reasons: The muscular posterior wall faces the esophagus.
The tracheal support is incomplete hyaline cartilage.
The carina identifies the main bifurcation.
questions.explanation: The muscular posterior wall faces the esophagus.

questions.question: Trace the central airway until it divides into two main bronchi. Which landmark marks this division?
reasons: The ridge at the tracheal bifurcation separates the two main bronchial entrances.
It is at the laryngeal entrance, superior to the trachea.
It bridges the open posterior ends of cartilaginous rings.
questions.explanation: The ridge at the tracheal bifurcation separates the two main bronchial entrances.

modules.title: Nasal mucosa and longitudinal airway histology
modules.summary: Identify olfactory versus respiratory mucosa and orient a longitudinal airway section.

topics.title: Separate olfactory and respiratory mucosa
body: Compare epithelium and the tissue below it.

Olfactory mucosa includes sensory neurons, supporting cells and basal cells with glandular and nerve profiles beneath it. Typical respiratory epithelium has cilia and goblet cells. Identify the region using both epithelium and underlying structures.

questions.question: Which finding supports olfactory mucosa?
options: Sensory epithelial cells with Bowman gland profiles beneath
Numerous goblet cells as the only clue
Hyaline cartilage rings under the mucosa
reasons: The combination supports olfactory specialization.
They favor typical respiratory mucosa.
This pattern belongs to tracheal wall rather than identifying olfactory epithelium.
questions.explanation: The combination supports olfactory specialization.

questions.question: Compare the two mucosae in the source image. Which combination supports the olfactory region?
options: Thicker specialized epithelium with glands and nerve bundles beneath
A multilayered keratinized surface with no lamina propria
reasons: The combination is typical of olfactory mucosa.
That pattern supports respiratory mucosa.
That is inconsistent with the olfactory region shown.
questions.explanation: The combination is typical of olfactory mucosa.

figure.caption: Practical source image · inspect it before answering

activities.prompt: Match each structure to its identifying feature.

topics.title: Follow layers along a longitudinal section
body: Identify the ciliated luminal lining, then locate the gland-bearing submucosa and the supporting hyaline cartilage segments.
In longitudinal view, periodic cartilage segments may look discontinuous. Use the mucosal surface to orient before identifying repeated profiles deeper in the field.

questions.question: What lies between the epithelial lining and cartilage and can contain seromucous glands?
reasons: Glandular profiles lie in the supporting tissue above cartilage.
Secretions enter the lumen, but the glands are within the wall.
The classic seromucous gland layer is deeper than mucosa and internal to cartilage.
questions.explanation: Glandular profiles lie in the supporting tissue above cartilage.

questions.question: Follow the luminal lining toward the cartilage in the longitudinal view. What are the clustered profiles between them?
reasons: Their position above the cartilage and lobular appearance support the identification.
The supportive cartilage forms deeper segments, separate from glandular profiles.
Cilia are at the apical epithelial surface rather than in submucosa.
questions.explanation: Their position above the cartilage and lobular appearance support the identification.
