modules.title: Cardiac cycle · Physiology lab
modules.summary: Read pressure curves, relate valve events and interpret the supplied valvular lesions.

topics.title: Valve events and pressure–volume phases
body: Start with the axes and pressure relationships. The mitral valve closes when LV pressure rises above LA pressure. The aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure. Aortic closure begins relaxation; mitral opening begins ventricular filling.

In the normal schematic loop, filling increases volume from ESV to EDV. Isovolumetric contraction raises pressure at fixed EDV with both valves shut. Ejection reduces volume after aortic opening. Isovolumetric relaxation lowers pressure at fixed ESV. In a regurgitant valve lesion the perfectly sealed isovolumetric assumption no longer holds.
keyPoints: Compare pressures across a valve before naming its state.
Filling and ejection change volume; normal isovolumetric phases do not.
Systole begins at mitral closure and ends at aortic closure.

questions.question: In a normal LV, which phase has rising pressure, fixed EDV and both valves closed?
reasons: The ventricle develops pressure before the aortic valve opens, without changing volume.
Rapid filling increases ventricular volume after mitral opening.
Ejection reduces volume while the aortic valve is open.
Relaxation has falling pressure and begins at ESV, not EDV.
questions.explanation: The ventricle develops pressure before the aortic valve opens, without changing volume.

questions.question: What pressure change normally opens the aortic valve?
options: LA pressure rises above LV pressure
Aortic pressure rises above LV pressure
LV pressure rises above aortic pressure
reasons: That gradient opens the mitral valve during filling.
That reversed gradient favors aortic valve closure.
Right-to-left atrial pressure does not normally open the aortic valve.
A positive LV-to-aortic pressure gradient initiates forward ejection.
questions.explanation: A positive LV-to-aortic pressure gradient initiates forward ejection.

questions.question: Which event begins normal isovolumetric relaxation?
reasons: Aortic opening begins ventricular ejection.
Mitral opening ends isovolumetric relaxation and starts filling.
Aortic closure ends ejection; pressure then falls before mitral opening.
Mitral closure begins isovolumetric contraction.
questions.explanation: Aortic closure ends ejection; pressure then falls before mitral opening.

questions.question: During ventricular filling, which valve pair is normally present?
reasons: This is the normal ejection configuration, not filling.
Blood enters from LA through the open mitral valve while aortic backflow is prevented.
Both valves open would not represent the normal filling phase.
Both valves closed describes an isovolumetric phase.
questions.explanation: Blood enters from LA through the open mitral valve while aortic backflow is prevented.

questions.question: Why should a normal rectangular-sided PV loop not be assumed in severe mitral regurgitation?
options: Regurgitant flow disrupts the sealed isovolumetric phases
Blood becomes incompressible only in regurgitation
The aortic valve is permanently absent
reasons: An incompetent mitral valve permits LV volume change through backflow while a normal valve would be shut.
Blood is already nearly incompressible in normal cardiac physiology.
Mitral regurgitation does not imply an absent aortic valve.
The LV still contracts; abnormal flow changes the pressure–volume relationship.
questions.explanation: An incompetent mitral valve permits LV volume change through backflow while a normal valve would be shut.

figure.caption: Valve events and pressure–volume phases · supplied practical, p/slide 4

topics.title: Recognize the four supplied valve lesions
body: Mitral regurgitation produces a prominent LA v-wave during ventricular systole because blood enters LA from LV. Aortic stenosis produces a large systolic pressure difference between LV and aorta. Mitral stenosis raises LA pressure relative to LV during diastolic filling.

Aortic regurgitation causes aortic-to-LV flow in diastole, reducing aortic diastolic pressure and increasing LV volume loading. The source case has a wide pulse pressure. Two worksheet stems reverse systole and diastole; the reviewed explanations here use the correct flow direction and phase.
keyPoints: MR: systolic atrial v-wave.
AS: systolic LV–aortic pressure gradient.
MS: diastolic LA–LV pressure gradient.
AR: diastolic runoff and wide pulse pressure.

questions.question: A giant LA v-wave occurs during ventricular systole. Which lesion best fits?
reasons: Mitral stenosis mainly obstructs forward diastolic atrial emptying.
Aortic stenosis mainly creates a systolic LV-to-aortic gradient.
Atrial contraction produces the a-wave near the end of diastole, not a giant systolic v-wave.
Mitral incompetence allows systolic regurgitation from LV to LA, enlarging the v-wave.
questions.explanation: Mitral incompetence allows systolic regurgitation from LV to LA, enlarging the v-wave.

questions.question: LV systolic pressure greatly exceeds aortic systolic pressure. What is the obstructed valve?
reasons: Tricuspid obstruction affects right atrial emptying into RV.
Pulmonary obstruction causes an RV-to-pulmonary artery pressure gradient.
A narrowed LV outflow valve requires extra pressure to drive ejection into the aorta.
Mitral stenosis obstructs LA-to-LV diastolic filling.
questions.explanation: A narrowed LV outflow valve requires extra pressure to drive ejection into the aorta.

questions.question: LA pressure stays high during diastole because atrial emptying is obstructed. What lesion fits?
reasons: Pulmonary stenosis involves right ventricular outflow, not LA emptying.
A narrowed mitral orifice blocks diastolic flow from LA into LV.
Systolic backflow explains an enlarged v-wave rather than the specified filling obstruction.
Aortic stenosis impedes ventricular outflow during systole.
questions.explanation: A narrowed mitral orifice blocks diastolic flow from LA into LV.

questions.question: Why can aortic diastolic pressure fall markedly in aortic regurgitation?
options: Blood runs back from aorta into LV in diastole
Mitral inflow closes all systemic arteries
The RV empties into the aorta
Atrial systole stops all aortic flow
reasons: The incompetent aortic valve permits diastolic runoff into the ventricle.
Mitral inflow does not close the systemic arterial tree.
The RV normally ejects through the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta.
Atrial contraction does not explain aortic-to-LV diastolic regurgitation.
questions.explanation: The incompetent aortic valve permits diastolic runoff into the ventricle.

questions.question: Which lesion chiefly creates the source case pattern of160/40 mmHg and increased LV volume load?
reasons: Mitral stenosis reduces LV filling and does not produce this characteristic aortic runoff.
Aortic stenosis creates an ejection gradient and often a smaller pulse pressure.
A competent closed valve prevents the described diastolic return into LV.
Aortic regurgitation combines diastolic runoff with an enlarged ejected volume and wide pulse pressure.
questions.explanation: Aortic regurgitation combines diastolic runoff with an enlarged ejected volume and wide pulse pressure.

figure.caption: Recognize the four supplied valve lesions · supplied practical, p/slide 2

topics.title: SV, EF, CO and pressure calculations
body: Use the supplied quantities with units: SV=EDV−ESV; EF=SV/EDV×100%; CO=HR×SV. EDV120mL, ESV50mL and HR70/min give SV70mL, EF58.3% and CO4.9L/min.

Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic BP. At a normal resting rate MAP is approximately DBP plus one-third pulse pressure. An acute rise in afterload tends to increase ESV and reduce SV when other factors are held fixed; greater contractility tends to reduce ESV. These are controlled comparisons, not fixed numerical diagnostic thresholds.
keyPoints: Convert mL/min to L/min by dividing by1000.
EF is a fraction of EDV, not ESV.
State which variables are held constant.

questions.question: EDV is120mL and ESV is50mL. What is stroke volume?
reasons: 50mL is the residual end-systolic volume.
120mL is the end-diastolic volume before ejection.
SV equals120−50=70mL for this beat.
Adding EDV and ESV does not give ejected volume.
questions.explanation: SV equals120−50=70mL for this beat.

questions.question: For EDV120mL and SV70mL, what is EF?
reasons: A stroke volume in mL cannot simply be read as the percentage EF.
EF is70/120×100=58.3 percent.
That reverses numerator and denominator, producing an impossible ordinary ejection fraction.
41.7 percent is ESV/EDV for the stated volumes.
questions.explanation: EF is70/120×100=58.3 percent.

questions.question: HR70/min and SV70mL give which CO?
reasons: 70×70=4900mL/min, equivalent to4.9L/min.
This is a factor-of-ten conversion error.
This result divides by an extra factor of ten.
Adding HR and SV is invalid and mixes unlike units.
questions.explanation: 70×70=4900mL/min, equivalent to4.9L/min.

questions.question: BP90/60mmHg gives which approximate resting MAP?
reasons: 30mmHg is the pulse pressure, not MAP.
75mmHg is the arithmetic mean of SBP and DBP, not this approximation.
Adding the two pressures does not estimate mean arterial pressure.
MAP≈60+(90−60)/3=70mmHg at a normal resting rate.
questions.explanation: MAP≈60+(90−60)/3=70mmHg at a normal resting rate.

questions.question: At unchanged EDV120mL, ESV rises from50 to80mL. What happens to EF?
reasons: With the same EDV but greater residual volume, less blood is ejected.
ESV in mL is not interchangeable with a percentage EF.
SV falls from70 to40mL;40/120×100=33.3 percent.
66.7 percent is ESV/EDV, not the ejected fraction.
questions.explanation: SV falls from70 to40mL;40/120×100=33.3 percent.

modules.title: Echocardiography · Physiology lab
modules.summary: Orient the supplied ultrasound views, identify chambers, valves and septa, and explain echogenicity.

topics.title: Orient chambers in the supplied apical view
body: In the supplied apical four-chamber view, the ventricles are nearer the apex/transducer and the atria are deeper beyond the AV valves. In this particular display the RV and RA are on image left and LV and LA on image right.

Do not apply that orientation to every ultrasound window blindly. Confirm the view, identify valve connections and use the supplied image labels. Tricuspid connects RA to RV; mitral connects LA to LV.
keyPoints: State the displayed view before assigning sides.
Follow AV connections to identify atria.
Image left is not automatically patient left.

questions.question: In the supplied apical four-chamber display, the ventricle on image left is which chamber?
reasons: The source labels the image-left ventricle as RV in this displayed apical orientation.
The LV is on image right in the supplied image.
The LA lies deeper beyond the mitral valve, not at this ventricular position.
The RA is an atrial chamber beyond the tricuspid valve.
questions.explanation: The source labels the image-left ventricle as RV in this displayed apical orientation.

questions.question: Which chamber lies beyond the mitral valve from the LV?
reasons: RA connects to RV through the tricuspid valve.
RV lies across the interventricular septum, not through the mitral valve.
The aorta is reached through the aortic valve.
The mitral valve connects left atrium to left ventricle.
questions.explanation: The mitral valve connects left atrium to left ventricle.

questions.question: What is the main reason to verify the ultrasound window before naming chambers?
options: All views put patient right on image right
Window choice changes which chambers physically exist
Displayed orientation changes with the imaging window
Every black space must be an atrium
reasons: That fixed orientation rule is not valid across ultrasound views.
The anatomy remains; the imaging plane changes the appearance.
Apical, parasternal and sub-xiphoid windows depict anatomy from different planes and orientations.
Blackness indicates relatively few internal echoes, not atrial identity.
questions.explanation: Apical, parasternal and sub-xiphoid windows depict anatomy from different planes and orientations.

questions.question: Which connection identifies the RA–RV pair?
reasons: Pulmonary veins enter LA and do not define the right AV connection.
Tricuspid leaflets separate right atrium and right ventricle.
Mitral separates the left atrium and ventricle.
Aortic valve lies at LV outflow, not between RA and RV.
questions.explanation: Tricuspid leaflets separate right atrium and right ventricle.

questions.question: Which two chambers does the interventricular septum separate?
reasons: The interventricular septum partitions the ventricular cavities.
The interatrial septum separates the atria.
Mitral valve separates these left-sided chambers.
Tricuspid valve separates these right-sided chambers.
questions.explanation: The interventricular septum partitions the ventricular cavities.

figure.caption: Orient chambers in the supplied apical view · supplied practical, p/slide 7

topics.title: AV valves and septa on ultrasound
body: Locate each valve at an atrial–ventricular junction before naming it. The mitral valve belongs to the left heart and the tricuspid valve to the right heart. The interventricular and interatrial septa lie between their respective chamber pairs.

A single still frame teaches position; it cannot by itself establish the severity of regurgitation or stenosis. The supplied introductory deck covers structure recognition, not a complete Doppler diagnostic protocol.
keyPoints: Name valve plus connected chambers.
Distinguish septum from valve leaflets.
A still frame has important functional limits.

questions.question: Which valve separates LA from LV?
reasons: Aortic valve lies between LV and aorta.
Mitral is the left atrioventricular valve.
Tricuspid is the right atrioventricular valve.
Pulmonary valve lies between RV and pulmonary trunk.
questions.explanation: Mitral is the left atrioventricular valve.

questions.question: Which valve separates RA from RV?
reasons: The tricuspid valve prevents systolic backflow into RA.
Mitral is between the two left-sided chambers.
Aortic is the LV outflow valve.
There is normally a right AV valve at this junction.
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve prevents systolic backflow into RA.

questions.question: What separates the right and left atria?
reasons: The interventricular septum partitions the ventricles.
A mitral leaflet belongs to the left AV opening.
An aortic cusp belongs to LV outflow.
The interatrial septum partitions the atrial cavities.
questions.explanation: The interatrial septum partitions the atrial cavities.

questions.question: A thin moving structure at an AV junction should first be considered what?
reasons: Pulmonary veins enter LA rather than spanning an AV opening.
The sternum is outside the heart and does not form an intracardiac leaflet.
Location at the AV junction supports a leaflet before a more specific identification.
The septum is a chamber partition, not an AV leaflet.
questions.explanation: Location at the AV junction supports a leaflet before a more specific identification.

questions.question: What cannot be concluded reliably from one labelled introductory still frame alone?
options: The presence of the labelled ventricular septum
The quantitative severity of valve regurgitation
Which side contains the labelled mitral valve
The identity of a clearly labelled chamber
reasons: A labelled septum can be recognized anatomically in the still frame.
Regurgitation severity needs appropriate dynamic and usually Doppler assessment, not this still frame alone.
A correctly labelled mitral valve identifies the left AV connection.
A clear supplied chamber label can support anatomical identification.
questions.explanation: Regurgitation severity needs appropriate dynamic and usually Doppler assessment, not this still frame alone.

figure.caption: AV valves and septa on ultrasound · supplied practical, p/slide 7

topics.title: Echogenicity and transthoracic imaging
body: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound. Echogenicity describes image brightness from returned echoes. Anechoic structures appear black; hypoechoic structures return relatively fewer echoes and hyperechoic structures return relatively more. These are comparisons influenced by tissue interfaces, angle and machine settings.
The supplied TTE image shows a probe on the chest. The deck lists apical, parasternal and sub-xiphoid approaches. This uses sound, whereas a chest radiograph uses X-rays; a plain CT also uses X-rays.
keyPoints: Anechoic: black.
Hyperechoic: relatively bright.
TTE: probe on chest.

questions.question: A black fluid-filled region with virtually no internal echoes is described as what?
reasons: Anechoic describes the absence of appreciable internal returning echoes.
Hyperechoic refers to greater returning echoes and a brighter appearance.
A black ultrasound region does not establish calcification.
Radiopaque is an X-ray term, not the appropriate ultrasound description.
questions.explanation: Anechoic describes the absence of appreciable internal returning echoes.

questions.question: Which term describes a relatively bright ultrasound structure?
reasons: Anechoic describes a black region without appreciable internal echoes.
Brightness alone does not establish malignancy.
Fluid is commonly anechoic; brightness is not proof of liquid.
Hyperechoic means more echogenic than the chosen comparison tissue.
questions.explanation: Hyperechoic means more echogenic than the chosen comparison tissue.

questions.question: What energy is used in echocardiography?
options: A direct photographic view inside the ventricle
reasons: Visible light does not penetrate the chest for this examination.
Echocardiography is a reconstructed ultrasound image, not an internal photograph.
Ultrasound forms images from transmitted sound and returning echoes.
X-rays are used in radiography and CT, not ordinary echocardiography.
questions.explanation: Ultrasound forms images from transmitted sound and returning echoes.

questions.question: A transducer placed on the chest for cardiac ultrasound is which approach?
reasons: CT uses a rotating X-ray acquisition rather than this chest ultrasound probe.
Transthoracic means the ultrasound window passes through the chest wall.
Transoesophageal places the probe in the oesophagus.
Angiography uses vascular contrast and X-ray imaging.
questions.explanation: Transthoracic means the ultrasound window passes through the chest wall.

questions.question: Why should echogenicity not be treated as a direct density measurement?
options: Echo brightness also depends on interfaces, angle and settings
Brightness always gives an exact tissue mass
reasons: Acoustic reflection and acquisition conditions shape brightness, so it is not a simple density readout.
A brightness value does not directly provide tissue mass.
That universal statement reverses the common appearance of strongly reflecting interfaces.
mmHg measures pressure, not image brightness.
questions.explanation: Acoustic reflection and acquisition conditions shape brightness, so it is not a simple density readout.

modules.title: Thoracic radiology · Anatomy lab
modules.summary: Read PA and lateral chest images, orient axial sections and recognize the supplied abnormalities.

topics.title: Read PA and lateral chest landmarks
body: Orient the frontal film with the side marker. The source PA image labels the right contour SVC, RA and the IVC region; on the left it labels the aortic knuckle, pulmonary artery segment, left atrial appendage, LV and apex.

Identify trachea, carina, main bronchi, diaphragms and costophrenic angles. A lateral radiograph adds the heart, hilar region, thoracic spine and posterior costophrenic recess. A contour is a projected silhouette; not every chamber forms a distinct visible border.
keyPoints: Read the side marker first.
Right border: SVC and RA.
Left border: arch, pulmonary segment, appendage and LV.

questions.question: Which chamber principally forms the lower right cardiac border on a normal PA film?
reasons: The left atrium is mainly posterior and does not form this normal lower right contour.
The RV is mainly anterior and is better appreciated in relation to the lateral view.
The LV principally contributes to the left lower border and apex.
The right atrium makes most of the lower right cardiac silhouette.
questions.explanation: The right atrium makes most of the lower right cardiac silhouette.

questions.question: The upper left aortic knuckle corresponds to which structure?
reasons: The RV does not form the aortic knuckle.
The oesophagus is not the normal upper left aortic contour.
The aortic arch produces the upper left mediastinal aortic knuckle.
IVC is a right inferior venous structure.
questions.explanation: The aortic arch produces the upper left mediastinal aortic knuckle.

questions.question: Which structure is the ridge at the main bronchial bifurcation?
reasons: The aortic valve is an intracardiac outflow structure.
The carina is the ridge where the trachea divides into main bronchi.
The cardiac apex is a ventricular surface landmark.
The cupula is the cervical extension of parietal pleura.
questions.explanation: The carina is the ridge where the trachea divides into main bronchi.

questions.question: Which chamber contributes most to the left lower cardiac border and apex?
reasons: The LV forms most of the lower left border and cardiac apex.
The RA contributes to the right contour.
The LA mainly forms the posterior base of the heart.
The RV is principally anterior and does not form the normal apex.
questions.explanation: The LV forms most of the lower left border and cardiac apex.

questions.question: What is an added purpose of the lateral chest radiograph in this lab?
options: Replace the need to recognize anatomical projections
Recognize structures including the thoracic spine and posterior costophrenic region
reasons: Side markers still refer to the patient and must not be reversed.
Understanding projections is essential to interpreting either view.
An opacity is not enough to determine that fluid is blood.
The lateral view supplies depth information about the heart, hila, spine and diaphragmatic recesses.
questions.explanation: The lateral view supplies depth information about the heart, hila, spine and diaphragmatic recesses.

figure.caption: Read PA and lateral chest landmarks · supplied practical, p/slide 3

topics.title: Orient axial CT and sections
body: Axial chest images are conventionally viewed from below, as if looking from the patient’s feet: patient right is image left and anterior is at the top. Verify any markers and correlate the numbered CT with the corresponding anatomical section.

At the arch level identify aorta, SVC, azygos, trachea and oesophagus. More inferiorly identify ascending and descending aorta, pulmonary trunk, main bronchi and heart chambers. The source supplies numbered keys at each level; the same number does not necessarily represent the same structure on different slices.
keyPoints: Maintain patient-side orientation.
Identify the level before interpreting numbers.
Match chamber and valve connections on cardiac slices.

questions.question: On a standard axial chest CT display, patient right lies where?
reasons: Right-left orientation is different from anterior-posterior position.
The convention is to view axial sections from below, making patient right appear on image left.
That is the opposite of the standard axial viewing convention.
Image top ordinarily represents anterior, not patient right.
questions.explanation: The convention is to view axial sections from below, making patient right appear on image left.

questions.question: Which structure is usually posterior to the trachea in the source superior mediastinal sections?
reasons: The oesophagus lies behind the trachea in this anatomical region.
The sternum is anterior to the mediastinum.
Anterior skin is superficial to the chest wall, not behind the trachea.
The ascending aorta is not a universal posterior tracheal neighbour.
questions.explanation: The oesophagus lies behind the trachea in this anatomical region.

questions.question: At the cardiac level, which valve connects the source labels RA and RV?
reasons: Mitral is the left AV valve.
Aortic is the LV outflow valve.
Pulmonary is the RV outflow valve.
The right AV connection contains the tricuspid valve.
questions.explanation: The right AV connection contains the tricuspid valve.

questions.question: Why must the slice level be established before using a numbered key?
options: A CT has no anatomical level
Numbers are local labels that can name different structures on another slice
All numbers always refer to vertebral levels
reasons: The labelled CT anatomy is not a measure of ultrasound echogenicity.
An axial CT represents an anatomical section at a particular level.
Each image has its own numbering scheme, so correspondence cannot be carried across blindly.
These teaching labels are not all vertebral-level numbers.
questions.explanation: Each image has its own numbering scheme, so correspondence cannot be carried across blindly.

questions.question: Which vessel is posterior on the patient’s left near the vertebral body on lower thoracic slices?
reasons: SVC is a right-sided venous structure.
The descending thoracic aorta lies posteriorly on the left side of the vertebral region.
Ascending aorta is a more anterior vessel.
The pulmonary trunk is anterior/central rather than the posterior left aortic position.
questions.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta lies posteriorly on the left side of the vertebral region.

figure.caption: Orient axial CT and sections · supplied practical, p/slide 14

topics.title: Pleural air, fluid and apical lesions
body: The supplied pneumothorax image shows pleural air outside a displaced lung margin with loss of normal peripheral lung markings. The fluid image is labelled hemothorax by the source, but a radiograph alone cannot establish that an effusion is blood.

An apical lesion may involve the sympathetic pathway and produce Horner syndrome. The images support recognizing the location and discussing relations; they do not independently prove malignancy, bleeding or tension physiology.
keyPoints: Pneumothorax: pleural air and displaced lung edge.
Opacity alone cannot identify fluid composition.
Apical lesions can involve the sympathetic pathway.

questions.question: What finding supports pneumothorax in the supplied image?
options: Peripheral pleural air lacking lung markings beyond a displaced lung edge
A normal vascular tree reaching the chest wall everywhere
A discrete valve leaflet on ultrasound
reasons: BP alone does not establish pneumothorax.
Air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall and lacks normal pulmonary markings.
Normal markings extending throughout the suspected region argue against that pleural-air interpretation.
A valve leaflet is unrelated to diagnosing pleural air on a chest radiograph.
questions.explanation: Air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall and lacks normal pulmonary markings.

questions.question: The source fluid film is labelled hemothorax. What additional caution is correct?
options: A radiograph alone does not prove the fluid is blood
Every white hemithorax contains only blood
Hemothorax means air in the pleural cavity
The image demonstrates an intracardiac septal defect
reasons: Clinical context and sometimes pleural fluid assessment are needed to establish blood as the content.
Opacity can arise from several processes and fluid types.
Air in the pleural cavity is pneumothorax.
An opaque pleural region does not demonstrate a cardiac septal defect.
questions.explanation: Clinical context and sometimes pleural fluid assessment are needed to establish blood as the content.

questions.question: An apical mass may cause Horner syndrome by affecting which pathway?
options: Optic nerve inside the pleural cavity
reasons: Phrenic damage primarily affects diaphragmatic motor function, not the full Horner pattern.
The corticospinal tract is not a tract within lung tissue.
The optic nerve is not located in the pleural cavity.
The source highlights the relation between apical lesions and the sympathetic pathway.
questions.explanation: The source highlights the relation between apical lesions and the sympathetic pathway.

questions.question: In the frontal source image, an abnormality on image left corresponds to which patient side after confirming the marker?
options: Neither side can ever be assigned
reasons: A left-right location does not define a posterior surface.
Correct markers and orientation permit side identification.
The displayed frontal image is viewed facing the patient; the marker should confirm side.
Image left and patient left are not interchangeable.
questions.explanation: The displayed frontal image is viewed facing the patient; the marker should confirm side.

questions.question: Can the supplied pneumothorax still image alone establish tension physiology?
options: No; clinical and additional imaging findings are needed
Yes, every pneumothorax is under tension
Yes, the word pleural establishes shock
reasons: A tension pneumothorax can impair venous return and circulation.
Pleural air alone does not establish the pressure effects and physiological compromise of tension.
A pneumothorax is not automatically a tension pneumothorax.
A location term does not establish shock.
questions.explanation: Pleural air alone does not establish the pressure effects and physiological compromise of tension.
